subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Mr. J. T. THORSON (Selkirk) moved that the third report of the special committee on war expenditures, presented to the house on June 4, be now concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when the special committee on war expenditures began its study of the reference to it, it was somewhat awed at the vastness of the territory upon which it had entered. The territory was uncharted, and a great deal of preliminary exploratory work had to be done. Then, later, specific subjects of inquiry were suggested to the committee by members of the house, and from various sources; and as the inquiry proceeded the fields of exploration of possible economies began to become more clear.
May I give an illustration of the manner in which the inquiry clarified itself as it proceeded. When we were studying the subject of financial controls over army, navy and air force expenditures it became clear to us, through the study of that subject, that there were certain fields of possible economy that should be further explored. It is indicated in our report to the house that parliament looks at the war expenditures for the first time when the war appropriation bill is before the house. The war appropriation bill is based1 on estimates that are presented through the departments to the treasury board and to council, and then to parliament. It was disclosed to us that these estimates are largely based upon war establishments, and the operations of war establishments, and matters that are incidental to war establishments. It was further disclosed to us that war establishments
consist mainly of persons, plant and equipment. It therefore became clear that there were fields of exploration of possible economies back of the estimates themselves.
Three large possible fields of economy were opened up: one relating to all questions of personnel and the most efficient and economic use of personnel; a second relating to construction projects and all that is involved in the preliminary study of construction projects and construction programmes, and a third relating to equipment, munitions and supply. The desirability of making a study of these three main factors that enter into a war establishment before the war establishment itself is finally approved and becomes the basis of an estimate became therefore very clear. It was for that reason that the committee recommended the setting up of an establishments committee in such of the defence departments as have not a committee of that kind. It is not always easy to review an establishment once it has been created; therefore it is essential that there should be the most careful review of all establishment proposals before they leave the department itself; for the establishment proposal becomes the basis of the estimate, and the estimate in turn becomes the basis of the appropriation that is made in this house. The committee therefore emphasized particularly the need of an establishments committee. I give this by way of illustration of the manner in which the fields of possible economies opened themselves up to the committee as it proceeded with its inquiries.
As the committee continued its inquiries it came gradually to an agreement on certain fundamental principles. There was some confusion with regard to some of these at the outset, but I think that these principles are now completely clarified in the minds of all the members of the committee. The committee was appointed for the purpose of examining all war expenditures with a view to reporting what economies were possible consistent with the execution of the policy decided upon by the government. The committee has therefore agreed, and is settled in its view, that it is not a public accounts committee. The house has already a standing committee on public accounts, and if there is any hon. member who thinks that a matter should be referred to the public accounts committee he has the right to ask that it be so referred, but if he does so, he must do so on his own responsibility.
The committee is not precluded from examining past transactions; indeed in that respect the reference to the Canadian committee is very much larger than the reference
3720	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
to the corresponding committee set up in the United Kingdom. But while the committee is not precluded from examining past expenditures, its only purpose in doing so is to explore the possibilities of future economy, and it has acted in that light.
Furthermore the committee is not a fact finding committee. It does not conceive it to be a part of its functions to approve or disapprove any particular transaction, or merely to find the facts with regard to a particular transaction. Its purpose is very much larger than that. Its function is to promote, as far as it can, economies in our war expenditures, to eliminate waste where waste exists, and inefficiency where inefficiency exists. In its search for economy and in its desire to eliminate waste and inefficiency it must not in any manner whatsoever, directly or indirectly, hamper or restrict the war effort of Canada.
The report presented to the house emphasizes the need for adequate and proper control of war expenditures at every stage, but it also stresses the importance of not restricting in any manner whatsoever the war effort of this country. May I quote what the committee says in that regard:
The application of financial controls over war expenditures must not be of such a nature as to hamper or restrict our war effort but rather in aid and furtherance of it. Indeed it is in that light that the subcommittee sees the importance of proper controls. Proper controls do not lessen the effective power of our armed forces. On the contrary, they increase it, for the economic use of our financial resources makes possible greater increase in manpower and the instruments of war and greater striking and defensive force.
The committee found it necessary to operate by means of subcommittees. There were many subjects of inquiry; indeed the special committee on war expenditures differs in a number of respects from any of the other committees that have been set up by the house. There are literally scores of subjects that require study and. investigation; indeed in this one reference to the committee there are many subjects involved, any one of which might well deserve a special inquiry. In fact, it was when the committee began to function through its subcommittees that it did its most effective work.
When the decision was made to continue the studies of the committee by subcommittees the committee also faced- the necessity of making a decision as to whether the sittings of the subcommittees should be open or in camera. It was urged that all sessions of the subcommittees should be open sessions, but this contention did not commend, itself to the committee. The committee did not accept that view. It decided that, in the

main, meetings of the subcommittees should be held in camera except as a subcommittee might otherwise itself determine. In taking that decision the committee was not seeking to hide any facts; it was not a desire for secrecy that prompted that decision. Secrecy is important for one purpose, namely that aid shall not be given to the enemy. Indeed that is the main purpose of secrecy in deliberations of this sort. But the decision that the meetings of the subqommittees should be in camera was not based, exclusively upon the need for secrecy. It was based upon the grounds of efficiency in the prosecution- of the task entrusted to the committee. Everyone in this house knows that the committee system of inquiry is not the most ideal system of inquiry. It has its shortcomings, but on the other hand it has also its advantages. The committee decided that the sessions of its subcommittees should be held in camera largely on two grounds. It was felt that in camera sittings would make for a more direct and a more concentrated approach to the subjects that were under investigation. There is a natural tendency of members when the press is present to make speeches. That is not confined to the members of any particular group. The making of speeches does not further an inquiry, and when sessions are held, in camera the number of speeches becomes very considerably limited and members apply themselves more directly and with greater concentration to the subject that is at hand.
There was another reason and a more important one for the decision of the committee that its sessions should be in camera. This committee is not a fact-finding committee. It is a committee for the purpose of promoting economies. In order to promote economies it must know where the economies are possible, and in order that it shall obtain that knowledge it must have the full and complete assistance of officials who are in the services themselves and know the details of all the operations of the administration of such departments. There must be the fullest scope for a frank discussion of what has happened and what can be done. There must be the freest possible exchange of opinion, because it is from that free exchange of opinion that the possible avenues of economies open up.
Then, too, it is well known that officials of departments when they know that the press is present and that every word that they utter will be published tend to freeze up and will not give as full an expression of opinion as they otherwise would. That is natural and human, and we all know that it is a fact.

War Expenditures Committee-Report
Our committee was impressed with the rapidity of the expansion of our fighting services. Perhaps I might give some interesting figures to show that. I shall give, first of all, the figures for the last year before the war, the year 1938-39 and corresponding figures for the present fiscal year.

speechtext: We have them all here this morning.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are all on record but, by way of illustration, the appropriations for the army services increased from $16,727,000 to $666,574,000. Naval service appropriations increased from $6,639,000 to $169,640,000. Air service appropriations increased from $11,688,000 to $386,003,000. This showed an immense rapid expansion of our fighting services. It would be amazing, Mr. Speaker, if in the course of that rapid expansion there was no waste, because the objective at the time was not economy. The objective was speed in expansion, and there was not, of course, the same cost consciousness as exists in peace time. Canada owes a very great debt of gratitude to the defence departments for the energy and the drive which made this rapid expansion possible. But now, Mr. Speaker, we can more easily and perhaps more intelligently promote economies than we could a year ago, when speed of expansion was the first essential. It is now our duty as members of this committee to promote these economies in so far as that is possible without in any way lessening the effectiveness of our war effort.
The committee has recommended a number of reforms of importance in our fighting services, believing that their adoption will result in very large economies throughout the services. The committee has sought to avoid invidious comparisons between the services. It has not sought to set one service against the other, or to make invidious comparisons between them. Nor has the committee sought to be spectacular in its findings, or to seek credit for any of its members. The committee could have made and announced very large estimates of possible economies; for the committee knows that large economies are possible, but the extent of these possible economies does not lie exclusively in the hands of the committee. I conceive it to be the duty of the committee to point out possible reforms, and to point them out in such a manner that they will be most effective and prolific in their results. It is therefore our duty to aid in the adoption of those reforms and supervise their progress and development; but the extent of the possible reforms depends upon the services themselves and the cooperation which
they will give, and upon the manner in which the loyal public servants in the departments, both civilian and service personnel, will carry them out. The promotion of reforms resulting in economies therefore requires the utmost cooperation between the members of this committee and the persons in the defence departments themselves, and the committee must act in such a manner as best to accomplish its fundamental objective, namely, the achievement of the necessary economies. The members have therefore taken this view, that for the time being it is their duty to submerge themselves in the objective which they are seeking to achieve; the allocation of credit for accomplishing economies is not in any sense the function of this committee.
The committee has really only commenced its inquiries. There are a great many subjects which require the most careful study. Many of them require immediate study so that if reforms are possible they may be set in motion as soon as possible. There are many subjects which still require further attention. Some of them have as yet not been studied at all.
May I be permitted to enumerate some of the outstanding subjects which ought to be further studied?
1.	Financial controls over army, navy and air force expenditures.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Only an interim report on this subject has been made, and a great deal of further work must be done.
2.	Review of headquarters establishments, with a view to eliminating duplication of functions where such duplications exist, and promoting coordination and the most effective use of personnel both service and civilian. That is a subject which requires a good deal of further study and thought.
3.	Army, navy and air force buildings construction; specifications and designs for such projects, and the inspection thereof during construction. Our committee has not as yet been able to commence its study of that very important and large subject, and it is important, particularly in view of the fact that there are large construction programmes still before us.
4.	Medical, dental and hospitalization services in the army, navy and the air force.
5.	Food and other supplies for the forces, the inspection and the distribution thereof.
6.	The salvage of all waste materials throughout the services. We have been able to make only the most preliminary approach to this vast and very important subject.

War Expenditures Committee-Report
7.	War contracts: the bases upon which they are let; centralized purchasing and local purchasing authority; capital assistance; and all the other subjects which are related to the subject of war contracts. We have made only a general study of this vast subject, and further study of it should be made.
8.	Labour relations generally. That is a matter of vital importance at this time.
I have enumerated only some of thfe subjects which require study. There are many others; indeed, as the inquiry developed and opened up, its ramifications became almost overwhelming.
It is desirable in the opinion of the committee that these important matters should be investigated as soon as possible. They are heavy subjects, difficult subjects. They require concentrated study and undivided attention. They are well worth exploring during the adjournment, when members of the committee will be free from their other political parliamentary duties and can give their undivided and concentrated attention to them. That is necessary; for, if economy reforms are possible, the sooner they are carefully studied and put into effect the sooner the results will follow.
The committee does not imagine for a moment that its task can be completed during the adjournment. Indeed, the task of this committee cannot be completed while the war is in progress.
The committee has been informed, and believes, that already it has been a stimulating factor in the promotion of economy reforms. Indeed the very existence of the committee is important in that regard. It is valuable to the services themselves and to the war departments generally that they should know that the committee is in existence and is studying the matters which come under those departments for administration. The knowledge that the committee is continuing its functions will be of considerable value in that regard.
Then, too, I think it will also be believed that the assistance which this committee can give will be greatly appreciated by those public servants in the war departments themselves- and there are many of them-who have been working loyally and faithfully for the achievement of economy reforms.
It is therefore the opinion of the committee that it should continue to sit notwithstanding the impending adjournment of the house. In that regard I should like to refer to the statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) when he suggested to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the formation of this committee. It was ms thought at that time that the committee

should sit continuously. I quote from Hansard, December 3, 1940, page 616. The leader of the opposition, in the course of his presentation of this suggestion to the government, said this:
We know that war is wasteful; we know there is great waste in this war, though I do not say intentional waste. I do believe, however, that a committee of private members of this house, sitting day in and day out during sessions and between sessions, could perform a very useful function in assisting the government at this time, and I commend this suggestion to hon. members.
This is particularly the case now that the fields of inquiry have been so clearly opened up and the need of economy reforms has been so definitely indicated.
It might further be suggested, Mr. Speaker, that a failure on the part of the committee to continue to sit will be a set-back to the reforms which have been already proposed, and that the members of the committee would in a sense, be "letting down" the persons in the defence departments who are struggling for these reforms.
If I might interject a personal note, I should like to express my very great appreciation of the splendid manner in which the members of the committee have cooperated with one another in the very difficult task that has been assigned to them. There are differences of opinion in a committee such as this. Differences of opinion are inevitable. But the very fact that there have been differences of opinion has, in my opinion, made the committee more valuable than it would otherwise be, for these differences have been honestly, and, may I say, very vigorously expressed; they are appreciated as necessary and helpful.
It will not be a pleasant task for the members of this committee to be sitting here during July and August, in the heat of Ottawa, giving concentrated and undivided attention to the very difficult problems they must face. That task will involve sacrifices, greater to some of the members than to others; but I conceive it to be a matter of national duty and I sincerely hope that members of the committee on all sides of the house will support this motion.
There are grim days ahead of this country. Our people do not fully realize the grimness of the situation that faces all who are engaged in this struggle. We must use our resources as efficiently as we possibly can; in the promotion of the efficient use of these resources I am convinced that our committee can perform a useful task. It cannot perform a perfect task, far from it; but it can perform a very useful one. I sincerely hope therefore that all members of the committee and all members of the house will join hands in further-

War Expenditures Committee-Report
mg the accomplishment which this committee has set before it, in reaching the objective which the committee has set for itself, that objective being that the people of Canada shall know that there is a body of men here in Ottawa who are seeking to ensure that Canada will get a dollar's worth of war effort for every dollar contributed by the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In the words with which the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) concluded, every member of this house concurs. He has told us of the vast field that has had to be covered, the still greater field that is open, and the opportunity of service which has been and will in future, in ever-increasing measure, be rendered available for those who are privileged to sit on this committee.
The committee itself will remember the circumstances under which it was set up. It was set up in consequence of a speech delivered in this house by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) on December 3, 1940, a few days prior to the adjournment. The house commenced to sit again in February and continued until March 4, 1941, before anything was done to set up this committee. As a matter of fact, vast as is the field of opportunities, great as is the challenge to this committee, neither the committee nor any subcommittee has so far sat for more than thirty or forty hours. We had an opportunity to start sitting from March 4 and it is well to remember that we did not start until well on in the month of May. I point that out at the beginning so that the picture may be before the house. Let me repeat, too, at this stage that the purpose for which the committee was set up was to enable private members to contribute something at this time to the war effort. I can do no better than to read1 from what the leader of the opposition said when the matter was first brought before the house. At page 615 of Hansard of December 3, 1940, the leader of the opposition is reported as follows:
I hold in my hand a series of reports of a select standing committee of the British parliament which was set up under the authority of an order of reference made on December 12, 1939, while Mr. Chamberlain was still Prime Minister and while there was an official opposition. The order of reference contains this: That a select committee be appointed to examine the current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
Let me interject that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) says the powers of the
committee set up by this parliament are greater than those of the committee set up by the British parliament. The only difference is this, that the word "current" was omitted. Further than that no change was made. The hon. member was frank to admit to-day that as far as he was concerned as chairman of the committee-and I agree with him to some extent-his attitude was that this committee was not to go into past expenditures. It was to view past expenditures not as a fact-finding body but merely for the purpose of coming to certain conclusions upon the basis of the experience with contracts that had been let prior to the setting up of the committee, and on that experience to recommend economies for the future. With that I will deal later.
The leader of the opposition continued:
Then it goes on and appoints a committee of twenty-eight members-and not one of them is a member of the government; they are all private members, and so far as I read the list of names, none of them are of international prominence. The committee has the usual power to send for persons, papers and records, and to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, and to adjourn from place to place. It was to be in effect a continuous working committee to examine current expenditures for war purposes having regard to the announced policy of the government. It had the power to appoint subcommittees and to refer to such subcommittees any of the matters within the jurisdiction of the committee. Such subcommittees so appointed were empowered to send for persons, papers and records, to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, and to adjourn from place to place.
As was pointed out by the member for Selkirk, the leader of the opposition, later used these words:
I do believe, however, that a committee of private members of this house, sitting day in and day out during sessions and between sessions, could perform a very useful function in assisting the government at this time, and I commend this suggestion to hon. members. It will provide an outlet for the energies of the private members who are anxious about the war, who want to make a contribution, who were sent here by their 'constituents to make that contribution but who find themselves frustrated-yes, that is the word-because they have no outlet for their abilities and their capabilities.	[DOT]
There is the background. The committee was set up, I repeat, to give private members an opportunity to serve to unify the people of Canada by reassuring them that such economies as can be effected will be brought about within the limits of government policy, by destroying rumours falsely circulated regarding phases of the war effort that would, unless checked, undermine public confidence. This committee should fearlessly reveal failure on the part of any department to practise necessary economies where efficiency would not be thereby curtailed. In short, the
3724	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
purpose of the committee, and the attitude with which we approached its work, was a desire to canalize the spirit of Canada by giving it the assurance that the sacrifices of the people would result in efficient action within the limits of government policy.
That was the attitude the members of the committee adopted; that is the attitude we hold to-day, for in these days of difficulty all of us, regardless of party, wish to serve. From time to time we may be assailed by fears that all is not well in this war effort on the part of the dominion. To those who are of that mind I believe the reading of what took place during the days of Napoleon will bring reassurance. The other day I came upon a statement made in the British House of Commons by Richard Brinsley Sheridan in 1808, which I think epitomizes the situation in the empire to-day and the attitude of hon. members of this house. These are his words:
Hitherto Bonaparte has had to contend against princes without dignity and ministers without wisdom. He has fought against countries in which the people have been indifferent to his success.
How applicable those words are to-day 1
He has yet to learn what it is to fight against a country in which the people are animated with one spirit to resist him.
That was the attitude taken by the leader of the opposition in the suggestion he made with regard to the setting up of this committee to strengthen and uphold the hands of the government at this time. Too often we think that this is the government's war effort. We on this side of the house believe that it is our war effort as well. In asking for the setting up of this committee, the desire of the opposition was to ensure that there would be no engaging in political wrangles; and we did not desire, nor should we desire at this time, to obtain political advantage out of wrongdoing, wasteful expenditures, and the like. All those things can come after the war.
Let me add, too, that I entirely agree with the statement of the hon. member for Selkirk that this is not a public accounts committee. Our purpose is not to find wrongdoing. Our purpose is to recommend economies for the future, but I do think the people of Canada are expecting more from us through the setting up of this committee than is within the contemplation of any of us. Under the resolution establishing this committee, the committee has no power to report wrongdoing to this house or to the country. The wording of the resolution bears out the construction placed upon it by the hon. member for Selkirk when he

said this was not a fact-finding body. We can only report upon economies, if any, consistent with the execution of the policy decided upon by the government.
We do say, however, that while we wish to secure no political advantage, we feel that when a committee is set up in this way, with eighteen members from the government side and only six representing all the opposition groups; when that committee sits behind closed doors, however outspoken and vigorous may be the ideas advanced by its members-and the hon. member for Selkirk referred to the fact that there had been, on occasion, vigorous expressions on the part of some of the members-the fact remains that people all over Canada ask, "Why are the meetings of this committee being held in secret? What is the reason?" No member of this opposition has ever taken the stand that there were not matters which should be kept secret, matters which might be of assistance to the enemy or which, if made public, might be detrimental to our war effort. But I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what possible advantage there is to the enemy if in time of war, as between 1914 and 1918, examples of wrongdoing should be made public, thereby assuring that participation in wrongdoing would be a pastime dangerous to those taking part therein? Going back to 1914-18, how often were charges made against persons high in public life and industry? More than once, and when those charges were made they were investigated publicly, and that did not do Canada's war effort any harm. It assured the people of the dominion, under the leadership of Sir Robert Borden, that wrongdoing merited the strongest condemnation, whether it was on the part of political friends or not.
Als I say, our attitude was that the meetings should be open, that the evidence should be heard in open session, except such matters as might be of advantage to the enemy. I would even go so far as to add what was mentioned to-day by the hon. member for Selkirk, the evidence of officials in the public service who might be fearful of expressing themselves if everything they said was going to be bruited abroad throughout the dominion. But I ask you again, Mr. Speaker: why should the evidence in regard to waste, overexpenditure and unjustifiable expenditure be hidden away in reports of the committee which are in the possession of the chairman only and not in the possession of the members of the committee? The chairman of the committee says there is no desire to "hide things". But when the committee sits behind closed doors the public is liable to suspect there is something to hide. It is unthinkable that the party in power has been collecting campaign funds from war contractors. Then why the secrecy? In the Commons, Premier King intimated that the only reason for secrecy in the taking of evidence was the prevention of useful technical information reaching the enemy. What would a committee of laymen be doing with technical information, especially a committee considering war expenditures?
Ten months after the last war started, the purchase of war supplies was under investigation by the public accounts committee, but it seemed expedient to Sir Robert Borden, the then prime minister, to continue and enlarge the investigation.
Then it goes on to say:
The government ought to throw the investigation wide open, except with regard to war secrets, if it -wants to satisfy the public.
I think that, generally speaking, represents the point of view to-day of the people of Canada as a whole.
We believe no harm would be done to our war effort-and we would certainly not want to d'o such harm-by pointing out where waste has taken place. We agree with the hon. member for Selkirk that there has been a great expansion of Canada's war effort during the last six, seven or eight months.

There has been a vast spreading out, and, as he says, it would not 'be for us even to suggest that in the desire for acceleration of the war effort there would not be instances of waste. But that is a different thing, Mr. Speaker, from waste or over-expenditure consequent upon a government declaration of policy, or upon agreements entered into by the government, and still in effect to-day.
Our attitude to-day, and throughout, has been to give every assistance in the committee to assure that there shall be efficiency and, to assure a dollar's worth of war effort for every dollar of expenditure, within the limits of the necessities and requirements of an accelerated war effort. But while we do not believe in scandal-hunting at this time, we do believe that in the interests of morale, and to assure the people that all that can be done is being done, and to prevent over-expenditure, the evidence that has been taken should be placed not only before members of the committee but before the country.
As I have already pointed out, we as members of the committee are not permitted to have copies of the evidence that is being taken from day to day. Somebody says, "Do you make charges?" No, Mr. Speaker, we as an opposition are just as anxious that *there shall be no wrongdoing, that no wrongdoing shall come out, that no cases of overexpenditures should be revealed, as any member of the government. So far as I am concerned I have forgotten political consequences, what the next election may bring forth, and I think that is the attitude of all hon. members of the house. Our paramount consideration as members of the opposition must be to refrain from obstructive criticism and fearlessly to offer constructive criticism. Not to have as an objective the winning of the next election; because it cannot be too often emphasized that unless this empire triumphs it will be a matter of small concern what political party we belong to. That, I say, is the attitude that we over here are trying to take, not the attitude of the classic aphorism of Tierney when he said that an opposition's duty is "to propose nothing, to oppose everything, and to turn out the government." We want hon. members on the government side to realize this, that we have a duty to the people of Canada in the creation of public opinion, that our sincere desire is to cooperate, and it is in that spirit that I advance in debate what I have suggested to-day.

The hon. gentleman is a member of the committee. He concurs, I am sure, in everything I have said in regard to our aims and purposes, and I should be the last to suggest that what he says in that regard is not true. But that is only a justification for not making the evidence public as it arises; it does not answer the point I have raised that we as members have a right to that evidence and to make it public before the country after we have come to a conclusion based upon both sides of the question as it has been placed before us.
I have dealt at some length with the question of secrecy; now let me refer to another aspect of the matter, namely, the setting up of the committee. I have already said that as to the general terms of reference and the purposes to be served by the committee it was modelled on the committee set up in Great Britain. But one slight change would have made the people of Canada feel that the committee was entirely free from the criticism that there was on the one hand an overwhelming government majority, and on the other, if I may use the expression, an overwhelmingly small minority. The committee was not set up the way the British committee was. There they set up a committee on which there was equality as between government and opposition, the government having a majority of one. Here a committee is set up with eighteen members representing the government side, four the official opposition, and, one each the two other opposition groups. Why should a committee not be set up that would indicate to the people of Canada the desire to give leadership at this time regardless of political consequences? Let the government say to us: We will give numerical equality with the opposition, retaining to ourselves the majority by having a chairman and vice-chairman of the committee. Would there be anything wrong with that?
The hon. member for Selkirk says that this is not an ordinary committee, that it is an extraordinary committee and I agree. Justification there might be by tradition for inequalities in ordinary committees, but there can be no such justification for a committee set up with the high purpose and the firm resolution that politics shall be divorced therefrom. We are all human, and if you pile up against the opposition a majority of four to one, however fair the meetings, there is left in the country as a whole the idea that the committee is overwhelmingly against bringing out recommendations that ought to be brought

War Expenditures Committee-Report
out. I plead with the government now, if we are going to continue the work of this committee-and work of great importance has been done and very considerable economies have been effected, although as yet it has only covered the fringe-to forget political considerations, forget the rules of the house, if you will, based upon tradition, and equalize the representation of the government and the opposition, giving to the government the right to control the committee through the chairman and vice-chairman. Because as the hon. gentleman has said, the work of this committee is very trying. It requires hours of labour, it requires concentration. Yet what is our position? The government members may leave from time to time; they can spell one another off; we continue to sit if we wish to be represented. Therefore I suggest, first, remove the veil of secrecy, subject to imposing it when the public interest demands; second, equalize the representation of government and opposition members.
I come now to another matter. It has been said, according to the press, that members of the committee are to receive $15 a day for an allowance for expenses in respect to sittings held between sessions of the house. I think I express the view of all hon. members on this side of the house when I say that to make such an allowance would be a dangerous thing for the morale of this nation. It would encourage the spreading of all kinds of rumours if we in this house, while advocating the necessity for sacrifice, when it came to a practical application of the doctrine, should forget all about our professions in that regard. My suggestion is that we as members of this committee-most of us were anxious to be on it for the opportunity it offered to serve, give a lead to the people at this time- regardless of our financial position, should not be placed in the position of saying to the people of Canada that we think we ought to have an allowance additional to our indemnities for serving on the war expenditures committee. For, after all, as members of parliament our duty as members extends throughout the year and is not confined to the period during which we sit in the house.
I have criticized in the past large expenditures for per diem allowances made to others. Can any hon. member who has taken a similar stand justify before the people of Canada what we have criticized in others. As I see it, our primary duty as members of this house is to assist in making the laws-although our legislative and deliberative functions have been considerably curtailed and are rapidly diminishing by reason of war-but our great duty is to implant in the people of Canada a
wider measure of appreciation and faith in democracy and its worthwhileness. That faith must be imparted to our people. That faith rests on the definiteness of the decisions made by this parliament, on the leadership it gives and the course it maps out.
Twenty-four members on a committee- $360 a day. Do that, and all over this dominion there will be the feeling that we in this house have let the people down. What do I suggest? I know the difficulties. The solution as I see it is this. We cannot, we dare not, at this time place ourselves in a position of accepting a per diem allowance. But the government might see fit to increase the membership of the committee along the lines I have indicated, and then we could set up subcommittees on a territorial basis instead of on a basis of subject matter. The proper division should be based on air, army and navy, and supply-at least that was the original intention-but to-day it is on the basis of subject matter. Set up subcommittees on a territorial basis. Every province has a certain number of representatives, and we can afford to meet in a provincial committee and investigate any matter which the chairman may consider necessary or which we as members of the subcommittee consider necessary.
We have no authority as I understand it- and I raise this as my second point-to accept any allowance. An interesting debate took place in the British House of Commons on February 27, 1941, in regard to the old principle that a member of parliament shall not accept a "place or office of profit" under the crown. This, in my opinion, having regard to the definition, is a place or office of profit. The principle, hon. members know, goes back to 1705, to the Act of Succession. So rigidly has this principle been applied that for years it was impossible for a member of the British House of Commons to hold a commission in the armed forces of Great Britain. In 1914, the parliament of Great Britain passed a statute in order to enable members who had accepted commissions in the armed forces to continue their membership in the House of Commons. That statute is chapter 3 of 1914, and its operation terminated with the end of the great war. The pertinent section is as follows:
The acceptance of a commission as an officer in his majesty's forces shall not vacate and shall be deemed not to have vacated the seat of any member returned to serve in parliament, and shall not render and shall be deemed not to have rendered a person accepting such a commission incapable of being elected to, or sitting or voting in, the Commons House of Parliament.
The necessary amendment to permit of members of parliament being commissioned was passed at the outbreak of this war. Our
3728	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
governing statute, of course, is the act respecting the Senate and the House of Commons. And what does it say? It permits naval and military men to accept commissions and retain their seats in parliament. Strangely enough, it does not refer to the air force. Whether or not an amendment would have to be made to "the Senate and House of Commons Act" to permit members of the air force to retain their seats in parliament would be a matter for the Department of Justice. The act refers to the naval and military forces, not to the armed forces in general. I fortify my argument, therefore, by saying that, as I apprehend the law, members of the committee who desire to take this allowance will be placing the tenure of their seats in this house in jeopardy.
With these suggestions, and not having any ruling as to whether the evidence which was adduced before the committee should or should not be referred to, I conclude what I have to say. I again press on the government the necessity of accepting some of these recommendations. Their acceptance will pay dividends, Mr. Speaker, in the reassurance it will give to the people of Canada that the government is not relying on the traditional basis of representation on committees of parliament and that the overwhelming power of its numerical strength in parliament is being relinquished in the case of this committee. We are animated by one desire, namely, to serve, and if we agree to serve, as I think we ought to, on the basis of no payment or allowance, any difficulties in the way of some members coming to Ottawa could be overcome by establishing territorial limits for the jurisdiction of the subcommittees. From time to time these subcommittees could send representation to the central committee at Ottawa in order to place before it the point of view of the different committees throughout Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the war expenditures committee I wish to say a few words. I am not going to go over old ground, particularly that traversed by the previous speaker (Mr. Diefenbaker). Whatever merit there may be in much of what he has said, it is futile discussion at this time because we accepted the composition of the committee and its terms of reference when it was appointed earlier in the session. So long as we are willing to serve, unless we ask for the discharge of the committee, I do not think there is very much use in taking up the time of the house in putting forward suggestions which, however good they may be in themselves, are not likely to be accepted by the government.

The committee was formed on a basis having relation to the representation of each party in the house. Maybe that was unfortunate, because of the abnormal conditions under which parliament is operating at the present time. However, it was done, and we agreed despite that to work on the committee. We are therefore not on very strong ground in raising the point at this time, although it is one which the government might well take into consideration.
The committee, however, has worked very harmoniously. There have been differences of opinion, but no acrimonious discussion, and we have got along very well. Little partisan feeling seems to have crept into the work. If it did, possibly I was not sharp enough to notice it.

I cannot accept, however, some of the statements made by the chairman, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), as to the nature of the work of the committee. He has said that it is not a public accounts committee. With that I agree, but I believe it has to do work which a public accounts committee would have to do, and to that extent, no matter what you call it, it is a public accounts committee.
He has also said that it is not a fact-finding body, but a committee to promote economies. Well, you cannot promote economies unless you know the facts, and to discover the facts you must delve into the organization and the financial transactions and everything pertaining to the war economy. That, really, is what we have been doing.
Having said that I do not agree in these respects with the chairman of the committee, I should add that I got along very well with him. As a matter of fact it was a very great pleasure to work with, or under, him-whichever is the proper term to use. We had no difficulties, and I am sure that so long as he is chairman that condition will continue.
The question whether the committee should hold secret sessions was raised, also as to members of the committee not having access to the evidence taken at these secret meetings. It was something new to me to hear that any members had been refused access to evidence. Personally if I were denied recourse to any testimony taken at a committee hearing I should refuse to act until I got it. I cannot make a report except upon the evidence, and I cannot make a report on the evidence unless I am allowed to examine that evidence. I am sure there must be some reason for the allegation made by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that he

War Expenditures Committee-Report
was not allowed to see reports, and that it cannot be correct in its full implications. To me such a state of affairs is unthinkable.
There is a great deal to be said, however, for holding meetings of a committee such as ours without the presence of the press, and possibly without the evidence 'being printed. It seems to me that there are two ways in which we can give comfort to the enemy. One is by making public facts which he would like to know, giving him information which would be useful to him. But another proceeding would 'be just as valuable to the enemy, namely, the making public of facts or reports which would tend to weaken morale in this country. I think everyone will agree that the greatest care would be necessary in considering evidence of the former kind. As to what information would or would not, if made public, weaken morale in the country, there might be considerable difference of opinion.
I do not believe that any harm was done, but on the contrary a great deal of good, by having evidence taken in camera. There were witnesses before us who were anxious to give expressions of opinion, but would mot have cared to do so were they to be put on record. They desired that the committee -should have their point of view for what it is worth. They took the position that certain investigations they were making had not been carried to the point where they could be definite in their conclusions, but so far as they had gone they had come to certain conclusions which they wanted to communicate to the committee as being their point of view. I believe the committee should be in a position to accept evidence of that kind. We are not bound to act on anything we hear, but we are bound to examine it. Eor these reasons I think the committee was justified in hearing evidence in camera.
It will be noted that the report of subcommittee No. 1, which is part of the report, has been amended, and that the report of that subcommittee and the report of the full committee were carried in the committee on division. I was one of the members who would1 not agree to the report of subcommittee No. 1, either in the form in which it came first before the committee, or as amended; for that reason I had to vote against it. I also had to vote against the report of the full committee. But this represented only a part of the committee's report, and with the remainder of the report I am thoroughly in accord.
I believe it is in order for me to state why I could not agree with the report of subcommittee No. 1. That subcommittee had to examine, among other things, contracts with
civilians, flying clubs, associations and companies. Contracts were made by the government with certain flying clubs when these clubs had satisfied the government that they had sufficient capital to carry out their contracts. The amount of capital was not really large. The government provided all the capital and equipment and furnished the money for carrying on the work of these schools, apart from management and perhaps other small items.
What I objected to in the report of the committee was that a bonus of common stock was given to the shareholders of the stock in these flying schools, and dividends were paid on this common stock-stock for which the shareholders paid nothing. I considered that, and I still consider it, something that this house should not allow. It is a condition as to which the committee should make a definite report to the house, recommending that it cease at once, and the government should see that the committee's report is implemented. This short explanation makes clear my position with regard to the report. I wish to put myself quite definitely on record in the matter; I think it is wrong. The people of the country will think it is wrong, and if it becomes public and the government does not take action it will be harmful to our war effort. I do not believe this is the time for any company, let alone a company that is financed largely by the government, to be building up reserves to carry on work after the war. If there is work of this kind to be done after the war, the government can finance it, just as it is financing the work at the present time.
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer, namely, the sitting of the committee during the adjournment. I believe the committee has done good work already. The mere fact that the committee was appointed has had a beneficial effect on the service, and there is a great deal of work still to be done. Despite the fact that I would much rather enjoy the balmy climate of Vancouver during July and August than swelter in Ottawa, I believe the committee should sit. I think it, however, a mistake for the committee to recommend that the whole committee should sit. A much smaller committee would be better. I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that this smaller committee might more closely approximate equality in the composition of its members than the larger committee did.
I am not going to say anything about the per diem allowance. I made my position clear in that regard in the committee. I think we should try as far as possible to keep

The
appointment of this committee came before the house on March 4, in a resolution proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He sought to pattern the committee on a similar body which was set up by the British parliament to deal with various problems in connection with the war expenditure, but this committee is of a different sort. It did not follow the text of the British resolution.
The committee has held a great many meetings. I happen to be one of those who on March 5 strongly opposed its formation from the start, because the committee system as we have it in this legislature never digs up anything. Moreover, the government of the day has a large majority on the committee and they write the report. Everything that I said in the debate on Wednesday, March 5, in opposing the appointment of the committee, has proved true. This committee when it was appointed was expected to deal with war expenditures, past and present, and to suggest economies. Now I do not know of anything wrong that has been done, nor do I wish to refer to things that have been wrongly done, but the people are paying $4,000,000 a day in war expenditures, a large part of which is not for the war and will not amount to a snap of the fingers in beating Hitler over in Britain and other primary theatres of war, where the war will be decided finally and conclusively.
The committee has not adhered at all to the text of its reference. The chairman wrote to members of the House of Commons a day or two after the committee was appointed asking hon. members to come and give suggestions. One morning I went to the committee myself and saw the chairman-not to take up any of the time of the committee but simply to submit on a page of paper suggestions regarding what I thought ought to be done. One of the main questions which the British government has been discussing is that of transport, and I have never heard one word in that regard from this committee. One subcommittee over there deals with it. Look at our transport situation to-day on the Atlantic ocean; consider the shipping that is being lost, and the lives of numbers of our sailors in the merchant marine, off the Irish coast and elsewhere in the Atlantic. One of the main reports of the British war expenditures committee had to do with the investigation of that whole problem, but this committee has ignored it. I asked the committee if they

would investigate soldiers' insurance, free soldiers' railway transportation, and other matters, but nothing was done. They said it was not for them.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of nearly all committees is to keep members out of mischief. Of course the idea is to give them plenty of work to do so that they are good fellows during the session. But I wonder what committee has been really useful since first I became a member of parliament? Nevertheless members have worked hard on committees, have toiled long days and have spent sometimes restless evenings, and far into the night, trying to get some deep knowledge of the matters submitted for their consideration.
I join with other members who have spoken in complimenting the chairman of the committee (Mr. Thorson), the chairman of the subcommittees and the members of the committee for their painstaking efforts.
I am very glad to follow in this debate my good friend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who is one of the most popular members of the house. He has always been known as the soldier's friend, and I am sure that he could serve in any capacity with very good results for the state if his services

War Expenditures Committee-Report
should be required by the government. All his life he has been interested in soldiers' problems. He has done a great deal for the soldiers. He has the added distinction of having been mayor of one of the largest cities of Canada for the longest period during the war.
The committee whose report we are considering was appointed to examine into war expenditures. Before the chairman had finished his address this morning I sent him a note asking him what his definition of war expenditures was. It could be very broad, of course, if we were to take in all expenditures made for the war and the financial business that is done by this government or the Bank of Canada, or the foreign exchange control board for the government of Great Britain, and if other similar bodies were to be taken into account. But I shall not go as far as that to-day. I will be good and take the report itself only.
The chairman of the committee said that this was not an ordinary committee but an extraordinary committee. Its scope was defined in the formation of three subcommittees. At page 447 of the Votes and Proceedings of June 4, which contains the report of the committee, the Department of Munitions and Supply is mentioned as a central purchasing agency for the three departments of national defence, army, navy and air, and we are told that the committee had reviewed "the various checks and controls in the matter of cost accounting that are exercised". The checks must be departmental. Control is the function of parliament, the House of Commons and the Senate, which is totally ignored in this report.
The report goes on to state that the committee has studied "the manner in which the purchasing organization within the department is set up and functions and a general exploration of (1) the existing checks, (2) controls, (3) care and (4) supervision in the matter of procuring necessary munitions and supplies."
The report goes on to say:
Your committee next made a general review of the subjects of inspection of and payment for munitions and supplies.
Inspection, of course, is by the department concerned, and payment is by the Department of Finance. Then follows a sentence which is commonplace:
The object of inspection of munitions and supplies is to ensure that the goods supplied are fit for his majesty's service.
That is evident, and therefore, I shall not insist upon it. It goes on:
It is essential therefore that this function should be performed by persons independent of either of the contracting parties.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
Meaning that the check should be made by somebody who has not sold something to the department or by one who is not in the department itself. That is very good; I agree wdth that. That is the case with parliament. Parliament is independent of all these people who buy and sell. If parliament had taken heed of what was said at the time of the creation of the national defence purchasing board we would not be in a mess like this to-day. Why was the Department of National Defence mutilated when Mr. Dunning as Minister of Finance put the national purchasing board under his control. I was the only one who stood up against that proposal. Saturday Night, which has no colour now, said, "Pouliot is a Liberal." I saw what was coming, and I thought it absurd to put the national defence purchasing board, which comprised all purchasing agencies of the Department of National Defence, under the control of the Minister of Finance. It was a crime. So much so, that afterwards the department of munitions was created. The national defence purchasing board travelled from the Department of National Defence to the office of the Minister of Finance, and from the office of the Minister of Finance to the office of the Minister of Transport. Then a new department was created, that of Munitions and Supply, which is neither man nor woman-it is an Auvergnat. Here we are, in a complete mess.
Moreover, the committee has not seen that in the view of the house what was necessary was to check, not the Department of National Defence, not the Department of National Defence for Air, not the Department of National Defence for Naval Services, but this very Department of Munitions and Supply. But that was not done. Here we have a minister who buys everything for every branch of the army upon requisition, and delivers it, and what we are interested to know is what happens from the time the requisition is received by the Department of Munitions and Supply and the time the goods are delivered to any branch of the defence department. That is the interesting part, but nobody thought of that in the committee. The thing was so organized that the attention of the members was distracted by something else. Why did the members of the committee not look in the first place at the set-up of the Department of Munitions and Supply, which is on record in Hansard'! They could see that it is chaos-chaos from beginning to end. When I asked for information I could not get it. What I find most strange is that

IFar Expenditures Committee-Report
the chairman, in his second report-I quote from page 458 of the Votes and Proceedings- said:
It should also he noted that reliable statistical records are essential as a background for adequate financial control and the future policy and programme of the department.
Of course. I agree with him in that.
It is therefore the opinion of the subcommittee that such essential statistical records should also be under the jurisdiction of the deputy minister.
All right. I am for that. But there is something which is more important: it is that every cent of expenditure should be submitted to every member of the house; in the first place, in the report of the auditor general, which is the public accounts; and when any lion, member asks for information he should get it at once. The government would have much less information to give privately to hon. members if that were done. No provincial body, no municipal council, no school board, no public organization of any kind could stand if that information were not available to all without being asked for, as it has been for centuries past in England, 'and as it was for a century in Canada since responsible government was established.
I have taken the trouble to check this report from page to page. As has been stated, there are three subcommittees, one for air, one for medical, dental and hospitalization services, food supplies, and buildings construction, and one for headquarters establishments and financial controls. I will consider these in turn.
The committee itself started to work on March 12. From that date until April 8 it spent its time on organization; several meetings were devoted to this subject only. In a second period extending from April 30 to May 5 the committee prepared an agenda. From May 5 to June 4-the third period^-some witnesses were heard in camera andl this report was prepared. Now look at this, on page 448 of the Votes and Proceedings, which are before every hon. member.
No. 1 subcommittee was appointed to inquire into the following matters: (a) Contracts. Not contracts with other countries- no; "contracts with civilian flying clubs, associations or companies; (b) Airports, aerodromes and air force building construction, specifications and designs for such projects and inspection thereof during construction," That is all.
What was done with the British commonwealth air training plan? It was never submitted to the House of Commons. Hon. members were not trusted to take cognizance of that plan. Many times the government was 14873-236
asked to submit it to parliament for further consideration, but the request was refused. But how can this committee on expenditures study the question of air services without seeing that plan, which is the basis of our air effort? Perhaps members of the committee have had the opportunity to see it, but it was definitely refused to members of the House of Commons, and it was because the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) made a slight reference to it that the air minister (Mr. Power) said that "Hitler was his last recruit." It was a secret. But how can members of the committee be familiar with the whole air effort of Canada without seeing that plan? And if the members of the subcommittee have every opportunity to read that contract and study it and get information on it, how is it that hon. members who do not belong to the subcommittee or the committee have not had a similar opportunity? With all the respect I have for the hon. members who compose the subcommittee on air, I say that the study made by it is worthless.
I come to the second subcommittee, for war: (a) medical, dental and hospitalization services in the army, navy and air force. That is an essential study, (b) Food supplies for the forces, inspection thereof, catering and salvaging of waste. There is no mention of clothing in the powers which are given to the subcommittee. Although the subcommittee reached a decision on clothing it was not empowered to do so at the time it was created, but it decided upon it just the same. And here, sir, you will be plainly astonished. I remember the day of the funeral of the late Hon. Norman Rogers-a year ago-and I was scandalized to see battalions there who had no rifles, although according to the king's regulations no soldier shall attend a funeral in uniform without carrying his own rifle. There were perhaps a few soldiers who had rifles; most of them had none. It is important that we have some information about munitions and about equipment, not merely about food. It is essential that soldiers shall be well fed and well looked after, but it is essential also that they shall be well equipped and well armed. I have asked consistently about this matter in the house without getting a decent answer from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). *
So, there is no question of clothing, and moreover, no question of ammunition, because ammunition is under the direct control of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and it was left aside. I wonder whether the chairman of the committee did not have instructions from the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) not to touch that department.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will ask the hon. member to sit down. I do not want him to speak at all at this time. He will reply in due course. I do not want to be interrupted by anybody. My time is short and I have a lot to say.
How is it that this committee has not touched the subject of munitions? How is it that the committee has not touched the matter of equipment, except to speak of old boots and old clothes which belonged to the soldiers? Of course people have a right to know these things when they subscribe to the victory loan, as I have advocated that they do on many occasions, when I spoke in favour of it at Riviere du Loup a week ago and also last Sunday at Isle-Verte, which was formerly the chief town of my county. I am here in parliament on duty and not for my own pleasure. It would be much more pleasurable to me to be at home to-day. I want to speak freely, and I claim the same freedom that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), had during the war, when he was the editor of the "Liberal Monthly," and as any other Liberal members had during the war, and I am speaking on behalf of my people. Nobody will prevent me from saying what I want to say for the protection of the soldiers and in the interests of my own people.
The third subject of inquiry of the second subcommittee is army and navy buildings construction. Nothing about construction for the Department of Munitions and Supply; only for the army and navy. Why does not the Department of Munitions and Supply get into the picture so that we can scrutinize as through a magnifying glass all the expenditures which are made there? No answer. Nothing is said. Note also that there is nothing about construction for the air service; no questions about the building of aerodromes, except for civilian flying clubs, etc. No, not at all; just the army and navy. Of course, the soldiers are under canvas most of the time. They are in camps, they have just tents, which are not very expensive; that is the lodging of many soldiers during the summer. It seems to me it would have been vital to get some information with regard, to construction for the department of air, but the answer would have been that aerodromes do not come under the department of air but under the department of transport and therefore we cannot scrutinize that. A subcommittee was set up with regard to financial control over army, navy and air force expenditures-headquarters 
establishments and pay and allowances. This report is bilingual, even in the English text, because there are some Latin words in that text such as "syllabus" and "honorarium". My knowledge of the English language is limited, and I did not know what the word "establishment" meant. I had to look it up in the dictionary. I find that establishment means: Church system, established by law; organized body of men maintained for a purpose, as army, navy, civil service. This is the first time I knew that. Other members who knew it before were more fortunate than I am; those who did not know it have now the same advantage that I enjoy after reading that excellent, non-controversial book-the dictionary.
Let me ask this question: AVhy were the sittings of the committee in camera? The answer is given at page 448 of Votes and Proceedings. I quote:
It was the opinion of your committee that its members would obtain a freer expression of opinion from persons appearing before the subcommittee if the sittings were held in camera than if they were open sittings.
Expressions of opinion! Expressions of opinion where you can have people swearing at each other and contradicting themselves all the time. But the course with the ordinary witness is to have that witness take an oath and tell the truth, stating the facts. That would be the ordinary course, and then it would be up to the members of the committee to decide what conclusions should be reached after reviewing all the facts. It is not simply the knowledge of a lawyer, it is the knowledge of every man who has attended one sitting of a court, that witnesses are not there to deliver lectures. And the witnesses that appear before the committee should be there to inform the members of the committee as to the facts which those members have a right to ask for and decide upon later on.
This was done during the last war. My hon. friend the member for Lake Centre said something really appropriate. During the great war the committee that sat was not a committee like this one but the public accounts committee and eveiything was open. Miss McAdam's shovel came out of it; old horses, butter and all the rest of it; but after it was all over it had a very good effect: it prevented others from doing likewise and people were more careful. So long as people are protected by silence you can expect anything. I do not see why this committee has been sitting in camera. What can we know? We know only what is disclosed to us. We do not know anything about the evidence given before the committee; nothing is quoted. The only thing they say is that the quartermaster-general

War Expenditures Committee-Report
appeared before the committee to tell a little story; that is all. There is nothing with regard to the essential thing, which is the commonwealth air training plan. That is not revealed to us. The committee has not studied that contract, it has not studied contracts with any other dominion with regard to air, but only what I would call subcontracts with civilian flying clubs, associations or companies; if it did, we are not informed about it.
With regard to elementary flying training schools, I find the following on page 449 of Votes and Proceedings'.
The subcommittee has been informed that these companies are organized on a non-profit sharing basis as to all common stock and that their preferred stock, which is limited to $35,000, is restricted to a 5 per cent dividend annually. The practice has been for public spirited citizens, service clubs and municipal bodies-
I think that should read municipal bodies, service clubs and public-spirited citizens, in the third place.
-to raise the $35,000 required, and in some instances the money has been made available for this purpose without interest. The intention of the plan is that after payment of 5 per cent on $35,000 of preferred stock all profits which accrue from the operation of the elementary flying training schools will be the property of the flying clubs to enable them to sponsor civilian flying and generally to give leadership to civilian aviation after the war.
This is not a war project but an after-war project, and you will see how it works.
Under the form of agreement between the operating companies and the crown the latter provides buildings, aerodromes and all necessary equipment including aeroplanes and recompenses the company for their services under four heads, namely, management, operation and maintenance, flying hour costs and messing costs. Of these, management and messing costs are fixed, while operation and maintenance and flying hour costs are adjustable each twenty-four weeks, based upon experience.
And so forth. I have not the time to read it all, but I would call attention to pages 449 and 450. There are two payments, fifty cents per flying hour and 25 per cent of any residue that may exist in operation and maintenance and in allowance for flying hours, gas and oil, at the expiry of the contract. The crash reserve residue reverts to the crown. The report states:
The operating companies have voluntarily surrendered 50 per cent of the flying hour profits as from the time the intake of pupils was increased from 48 to 70.
That is for public-spirited citizens.
Increased intake of pupils naturally tends towards increased flying hours and an appreciable decrease in overhead costs per flying hour. The monthly profits of the said companies range from $318.32 to $942.54.
14873-236i
There is no average monthly profit quoted in the report. Here we see the difference between estimated cost in operating elementary flying training schools, on the basis of target price, $982 per pupil, and the actual cost to the crown as of March 31, 1941, which was $864. The difference between what is paid the elementary schools and what it costs the crown to train a young airman is $117.96. If there are forty-eight pupils this difference represents an amount of $5,664; if there are seventy pupils the difference is $8,260, which represents the profit made by the school. If the investment is $35,000 and it is not possible to make more than five per cent profit on the paid up capital, that interest would amount to only $1,750 but the return to the company runs from $5,664 to $8,260. There are other sources of profit, as hon. members will observe, but the minimum yearly profit is $3,816, while the maximum is $11,088, the monthly figures being multiplied by twelve. The report does not deal with air observer schools or airports, aerodromes, air force buildings, and so on; that will come later, because the committee has not had time to deal with those matters.
The second subcommittee was to study medical, dental and hospitalization services in the three branches of the service; the construction of army and navy buildings; food supplies for the forces, the inspection thereof, catering and salvaging of waste. The report states:
The plan of inquiry was to secure from the proper departmental officials the system of operation and control in regard to these matters-
This is information which is denied ordinary members of parliament.
-and to inquire as to how these departmental rules and regulations were being applied and carried out in military establishments in and adjacent to Ottawa.
According to the report these matters were not studied at any point other than Ottawa. Then listen to this paragraph, at the bottom on page 451:
The present ration list is largely the result of recommendations made by a committee of expert advisers on nutrition, dietetics, hygiene, household science, agriculture, etc., under the National Research Council.
Pork and beans made scientifically! The report proceeds:
Specifications of each item have been carefully prepared in the quartermaster-general branch and these are furnished to each firm or individual invited to tender.
And then:
The officers in charge of supplies at these depots make their demands on contractors in accordance with their immediate requirements.

What contractors? Who are they? No one knows; the committee did not inquire into that point. How do we reach the man who is the contractor? How do we reach the man who is the go-between for a department? Then the report goes on to say that inspectors go into the meat supply houses and stamp the carcasses with the letters "D.N.D." meaning Department of National Defence, but it is not the Department of National Defence; it is the Department of Agriculture that does it. There is no economy in that. It is an economic fiction. Then this committee went to Petawawa; they had a Cook's tour there and found everything O.K. in the whole country because they had seen Petawawa.
Then there is a reference to the orderly system. I do not wish to abuse your patience, Mr. Speaker, but just listen to this:
One decided improvement was noted by the subcommittee at Petawawa. The "orderly" system of messing is used there and in the opinion of the committee is a marked improvement over the "cafeteria" method. It permits of a much more inviting service of food and should assist in minimizing food waste from the tables.
An lion. MEMBER: Oh, oh.
