speechtext:
You laugh; I laugh, too,
because I find it very amusing. Then there are other considerations. The subcommittee confined its inquiry to the salvage of food waste and containers and did not deal with other matters under the heading of salvage of waste. But this is the recommendation:
It recommends that the general committee enlarge the subject matter of inquiry under this head to include all items of salvage including foodstuffs, oil, boots and leather goods, clothing, lumber, containers and other worn-out or cast off material.
The committee did not give the subcommittee authority to deal with the matter of clothing, but here they deal with clothes as "garbage." It is not garbage; it can be used. There are poor people who do not receive any unemployment relief who could use this clothing. I obtained a certain quantity of worn-out military clothing which was distributed to the unemployed of my town and the settlers of my district on New Year's eve. It made these people very happy, and they gave thanks to the Minister of National Defence, the personnel of the department, the Prime Minister and all the members of the government for the charity they received from that department. Their little children could not go outside in the winter time because they had no clothes; they were unable to attend school, and these worn-out articles meant a great deal to them. But since this committee has been sitting it has been impossible to get anything from the department, because these
IMr. Fouliot.]
Solomons have not yet reached a decision. They have had no time to study these matters.
According to this report the committee has studied the question of the distinction between civilian and service responsibility. Of course the responsibility is undivided. It makes no difference whether the books of the Department of National Defence are kept by men in civilian clothes or men in uniform; all these people are responsible to parliament, and it is up to parliament to decide what should be done. They are responsible under the authority of the minister, so that any distinction between service and civilian personnel is ridiculous. Of course the taxpayer usually is a civilian. I made the statement in the house that it was ridiculous to see men in several departments, especially in the Department of National Defence for Air, rendering civilian services but wearing uniforms and therefore receiving extra pay and allowances. The report mentions that matter and agrees with what I said. That is the good side of the report; I have not time to quote it verbatim, but every lion, member has read it.
We should get back to the policy under which the minister was responsible for all purchases made by his department. That is necessary. Ask the Minister of National Defence; he will not deny it. He is not responsible now; all purchases are made by the Department of Munitions and Supply. The minister cannot buy a cap or a badge for his department with public money. He has to go through all the red tape of the Department of Munitions and Supply, which he finds very embarrassing. Formerly the minister had full responsibility; that has been all changed, but I believe we should go back to the sound policy under which the minister was responsible to parliament for what was done by his department. That is all I have been asking from him. I do not wish to cause the minister any trouble, but I want him to be true to the parliamentary practice of many years ago,-the parliamentary practice that he supported until he came to act in this government for the last time. Every one knows it. It is the policy of Joe Howe, it is the policy of Blake-it is the policy of all Liberals, and not only of Liberals, but it was the policy of Sir John A. Macdonald. It was the policy of those who consider government something other than a corporate body. That is all.
I urge each one of my esteemed colleagues in the house to take the trouble to look at the report between pages 454 and 459 in the Votes and Proceedings, and he will realize what was in the head of the chairman when he dictated or wrote those lines. I have great

War Expenditures Committee-Report
esteem for the chairman of the committee, although I do not always agree with him, and I do not wish him to interrupt me. But the chairman could not find his way through, he could not find his way clear; he could not understand that system of departments suffering from elephantiasis, or big feet,-big feet that fall in corruption. When any hon. member reads the report he will see there is something wrong, and that an operation is necessary and urgent.
Of course, it is said with the precaution one takes when he does not want to hurt anybody. But if people have chosen to have military uniforms put on their backs, for profit, and for being better paid, then I do not see why the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) does not transfer them at once to the army, so that they may fill the Tanks for the filling of which he is calling 32,000 men. They should be the first to go. They have been wearing the uniform for some time, and they have been getting more money than they would have been entitled to, had they not been wearing the uniform; therefore those people, if they are not cowards, should enlist at once in the real service of Canada. I do not think there is a single hon. member who will oppose me on that. These people have been parading the streets of Ottawa in military uniforms. I say they should parade in tanks, in the same uniforms. Then the state could pay them for military service, and not for military service under false pretences. I am referring of course' to purely civilian services rendered by those in uniform.
This must be the reason why the chairman's report is obscure. He did not go farther and say all to the minister. He wanted to be mellow and to use white gloves. But I say brutally what he said in a certain form of language which I do not possess.
In conclusion, what is the use of discussing this matter when we have no detailed estimates from the Ottawa offices of the three war departments? They are only bulk estimates. We have no information-all these matters are of great importance. We have not the scales with which to weigh them. The only scale is the exact expenditure, and we do not have a record of it. We have no information, either, about the Department of Munitions and Supply. I said that when the minister was not in the chamber, and I repeat it now that he is here. How is it that the committee did not get any information as to armaments? Even if it was secret, we should have had the satisfaction of knowing that the committee had information about it. Why did it not get information about clothing? Why did it not get information about construction for the air service?
All this reminds me of one thing. Once I visited Holyrood castle, and while there I visited the room, which, I was told, was Mary Stuart's. The attendant said, "This was her bed." After a while he told me, "No, this was not her bed; it is another bed, but it stands in the same place as her bed stood originally." That is the story of the report. This is not a report of expenditures. The expenditures are made by the Department of Munitions and Supply, and from the smile on the minister's face, it would seem he knows that is true. Neither the Minister of National Defence, proper, nor the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), nor the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), could spend a cent without having the requisition first passed through the Department of Munitions and Supply. Purchases are made by the Department of Munitions and Supply, but payments are made by the Department of Finance. Therefore I say the Minister of National Defence, proper, and his two colleagues, and the other war ministers, are out of the picture completely. One of them may write a small requisition,-"I want a hundred uniforms." That is handed to the Department of Munitions and Supply. That department call 3 for tenders, or the order is given to a contractor or to a tailor. The goods are then sent to the Department of National Defence, or to the Department of National Defence for Air or the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. When they reach there, I presume another form is sent to the Department of Munitions and Supply, and that department in turn gets in touch with the Department of Finance. Then the Department of Finance makes the payment. Has any hon. member ever seen anything like that?
I should like the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) to be in a position to feed the soldiers, et cetera. I should like him to be responsible for the payments connected with all purchases of food, clothing and munitions. I should like his colleagues in the departments of National Defence for Naval Services and National Defence for Air to be able to do the same. Although the minister who until recently headed the Department of National War Services is no longer head of that department, I should like his successor to do likewise, so that we in the House of Commons would know with whom we would have to deal. In passing I would say that the Department of Munitions and Supply should be abolished, and the minister of that department should be made Minister of National War Services, if such is found necessary.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the hon. member from this group who served on the war expenditures committee felt it necessary to leave, because of illness at his home. Therefore it becomes my duty to pinch-hit for him. Not having attended the meetings of the committee, I am not in. a position to pronounce in any way upon the efficiency, thoroughness, spirit and all those fine things which up to the present time have been commended. I assume statements which have been made in this connection are all accurate.
I shall devote my attention to the general idea of having such a committee, and to making such observations as would seem to be fitting in connection with the establishment and maintenance of such a committee of the house at this time. I believe the idea of having the committee is good, Judging from what I have heard from our member on that committee I do not think I am immoderate when I say that the committee has done good work and will justify its existence.
In the first place, Canada wants no profiteers. I think one of the most malodorous relics of the previous war was the number of millionaires and profiteers which was created at the expense of the people of Canada. It is my settled opinion that Canada has never recovered from the maladjustments in her social, economic and financial structures induced by the abuses of the last war. We want no repetition of those abuses. I am not disposed to be ultra-critical of the government which conducted the last war, I just leave what I have said as I have said it.
In this war the number of orders is bewilderingly large. If the problems connected with getting material fabricated and delivered during the last war constituted a headache, then I think the problems connected with the task in this war must create a super-headache. To the ordinary citizen and the ordinary member of parliament the whole thing is simply beyond comprehension.
Again, the nature of the orders is forbiddingly complex. When listening to reports from our representative I have wondered how such a committee, constituted as it was and even sitting once a day, could possibly adequately examine a sufficient number of accounts to enable it to do the kind of work which we all wish it to do. I am not able to answer that question; I am going to leave it unanswered. But I think it constitutes a third reason why we need a committee of this sort.
To most Canadians war manufacturing is very remote. For example, the people in the prairie provinces hear about it as something going on in a far-away country. I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for having taken up so much time and having more or less bored the house by reading this long list, but I believe it has a significance which the Minister of Finance and the other members of the cabinet can ill afford to ignore. You can see why this whole manufacturing and ordering business is more or less strange to people in most of the provinces. As a matter of fact, two provinces are gathering all the plums and seven others are not, and I submit that as a fourth reason why we need this committee.
Another reason is that for a great many Canadians there is no hope of profit or even financial or economic gain from these contracts, but only the privilege of "paying the shot". I noticed that in that list there were very few orders for seven of the provinces; members will recall that the provinces that were luckless in getting orders are primarily agricultural provinces. The ruinous policy with respect to agriculture which is being pursued by the dominion government of to-day is adding a good deal more than insult to injury to these seven provinces while they are suffering from these other disadvantages. Just the same, those provinces are obliged to pay all these impositions which we have been discussing under the budget. They all have to pay all the impositions as a result of the tariff structure of this country. They are all suffering from inequitable freight rates. They are all called upon to give their quota of loans. They are all expected to give their quota of enlisted men. That, I submit, is a matter worthy of attention.
Another reason why this committee ought to be proceeded with is that people, in order to fight successfully, have to build up an emotional attitude which makes them think primarily of the safety of the state, and think in terms of patriotism. When one is in a mood like that he is not likely to be quite so critical of what is going on in a business way. It is all the more necessary that there should be a committee here looking after the interests of the people who are being encouraged to develop that emotional attitude of patriotism. Always there are certain ones who think only in terms of dollars and cents.
The great body of the Canadian people may be likened to the farm hands who have to do the chores, the rough, hard, exacting work out in the wind and weather. They need someone in the kitchen, watchful to see that they get their share of the cream and pie; someone alert at the wicket to see that they get their share of the deeds and the dollars. This committee should serve as that someone watching in the kitchen, wa tching at the wicket.

Up to the present time the committee has not, perhaps, considered it one of its duties to exert some influence on the minister with respect to the placing of war orders. But, I submit, if the economic life of this dominion is to be preserved in anything like a sound condition, careful attention must be paid, to this tendency to raise great loans and heavy taxes from seven of the provinces, to be spent in two of the provinces.
Of what the committee has already done I have no criticism to offer. But it does occur to me that the committee should be enlarged and it should be modified, with respect to numbers. They tell me that there are on this committee, 18 Liberals, two Conservatives-
Four Conservatives.

Four Conservatives
-I am glad to be corrected-one Social Crediter and one representative of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I submit that the numbers of members of the various parties on that committee open the committee to serious suspicion to start with. I am not saying that the committee has taken advantage of the preponderance of one party, but I believe that the ordinary man in the street, looking at these numbers, would be very suspicious; he would find it difficult to see why at least the number of members from the three opposing groups should not equal the number representing the government. I understand the committee is to be conducted on a non-partisan basis, that its whole object is to find the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. I submit to you that a member of the Conservative party is quite as capable of finding the truth, and recognizing it when he has found it, as a member of the Liberal party, whosoever he may be. I would even venture to suggest that members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and Social Credit parties can do fairly good, work in detecting truth and recognizing it when they find it. I suggest that there be a definite modification of the relative representations on this committee. May I point out that, with only one Social Crediter and one member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, it would be a complete impossibility to have each of these groups represented on each of two subcommittees.
It was.
I think the committee has done the best it could to give them fair representation, and I understand the device which has been used is that of allowing a member of the Social Credit group to

The motion before the house is a motion for concurrence in the third report of the select committee on war expenditures. Hon. members will have noticed that about a week ago the chairman of the committee submitted two reports, the second and the third. The second report contained the recommendations of the committee with regard to the work it had been doing, and to-day we are really concerned only with the third report. I would ask members to look at the wording of that report, because we are being asked to approve its terms. It will be found at page 460 of Votes and Proceedings, and in effect it asks that certain powers be granted to the committee by the house.
First of all, it asks that the committee, which of course means the full committee of twenty-four members, be authorized to continue its inquiry notwithstanding the impending adjournment of the house. Then it asks that the committee have power to adjourn from place to place-for example from Ottawa to Halifax, say, or to Vancouver or anywhere else in Canada. It asks for power to sit in camera or otherwise as it may from time to

War Expenditures Committee-Report
time determine, and for power to determine the manner and extent to which the evidence and proceedings shall be printed or typed, and furthermore to employ such secretarial, clerical and other assistance as it may deem necessary. There are two other requests. One is that six members of the committee constitute a quorum during the adjournment, and the other, that any subcommittee appointed by the committee have power to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house and likewise to adjourn from place to place.
These are wide and unusual powers, and I suggest that it is the duty of the house to consider carefully whether or not such a request should be granted. My opinion is that it would be unwise in the extreme unless drastic changes are made in this committee, in the set-up of the committee and in the way in which it carries on its business. In order to outline my reasons for coming to that conclusion, I would sketch briefly the background, the manner in which the committee came to be appointed.
This committee was modeled of course on the committee in Great Britain. In the last war of 1914-18 there was a special committee in Great Britain, and shortly after the outbreak of the present war the British parliament appointed a similar committee, on December 12, 1939, so that their committee has been functioning almost from the start of the war. It has had the benefit of the experience of the earlier committee which served in Great Britain during the last war.
We decided in Canada this spring that we would do likewise and appoint a similar committee, and on March 5 an order was made appointing the committee and giving it practically the same power as was given to the British committee, with one exception. The word "current" as applied to expenditures was deleted so far as the committee here is concerned. I quote from page 446 of Votes and Proceedings:
Your committee was appointed by order of the house on March 5, 1941, to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
In addition, we had in mind that there would be an opportunity to suggest ways in which the general war effort of Canada could be improved; that the wrork of the committee would disclose such ways. I do not believe that in following the British example we realized clearly-I do not think we stressed sufficiently-certain facts: in the first place, that the British committee was set up at 14S73-237*
the start of the war, and that in Great Britain they had had the previous experience in the great war, whereas in Canada the setting up of such a committee was an entirely new departure. Then we did not realize that in Great Britain the committee can get around the country much more readily. It can get to the defence centres, and subcommittees can travel and find out for themselves what is going on, whereas in Canada that is extremely difficult. But above all we did not emphasize the fact that in Great Britain there is a national government, a parliament which is not working on party lines, whereas in Canada we have the opposite. That fact should have been kept more clearly in mind.
In any event, on March 5 the Canadian committee was set up. Every member of the house will admit that there has never been a committee of this house of a similar type. It was something new. This committee was intended to be different; it was not intended to be just another committee. We thought that we were setting up a committee which would be entirely different and that it would have a great place in helping Canada to play her part in the war. We thought that we could set up a committee which would be quite detached in its outlook, although parliament itself was functioning on strictly party lines. I have reached the conclusion that we expected too much of human nature.
I do not mean any offence to any member on the government side, nor do I wish to question the sincerity of members on the government side who were on the committee; and I do not pretend that the members of my party or of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or of the Social Credit group have any larger endowment of sincerity than members on the government side. I do say, however, that this war expenditures committee has proved to be part of the Canadian parliament, which is functioning on party lines, and that the committee has reflected in its actions the attitude of this parliament, which is dominated by party politics.
That situation was made much worse by the fact that the government loaded the committee with government supporters. We understood that there would be a committee of fifteen, of whom nine would be government supporters and six members of the opposition. Instead, we got a committee of twenty-four, with eighteen government supporters, twice the original number, and only six supporters of the opposition parties. In other words, there was a loading of the committee to the extent of three government supporters to one opposition supporter. That alone made it impossible for this committee to carry on as members of this house had hoped it would;
374S	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
and, further, it meant that the subcommittees which were eventually set up were also overwhelmingly composed of supporters of the government. No more than two opposition members were on any subcommittee.
After the committee was set up, there was a delay before the work was started. It took a week before we had our first meeting and two weeks before we called any witnesses. Before the Easter recess there were several general meetings of the whole committee, and on April 3, when the situation was discussed, our chairman announced that he thought, when we returned after the Easter recess, it would be wise to divide the committee into five subcommittees. Hon. members will find that suggestion at page 222 of the proceeding! of the committee. The chairman suggested that there should be subcommittees on army; navy; air force; munitions and supply, and miscellaneous. That was following the example of the British committee, which has subcommittees on army services; navy services; air services; supply services; home defence services, and trade, agriculture and economic warfare, and I believe one or two further subcommittees have been added. I think this proposal of April 3 was the proper procedure to follow, and consequently there would be subcommittees dealing with the various departments; where any question concerned more than one department, the subcommittees could meet together, as is done in Great Britain right along.
Accordingly we went away for .the Easter recess. When we came back, towards the end of April, the whole plan had been changed. It had been decided that we would not divide into subcommittees allotted to the different departments, but that subcommittees should be set up to deal with specific subjects. I have never been able to understand why that change was made. I do not think it was a sound decision, and I believe it has greatly handicapped the work of the committee. That, however, was done, and at the same time it was decided that meetings of these subcommittees should be held in secret, unless the subcommittee decided to the contrary. That motion will be found at page 237 of the proceedings of the committee. The wording is:
That the sittings of subcommittees be in camera except as the subcommittee may otherwise from time to time determine. . . .
The members of the Conservative party suggested that the question of secrecy should be left entirely to the subcommittees, which should decide at each meeting whether or not that meeting should be held in camera. Instead, however, the majority of the committee decided that all meetings of the subtMr. Green.]
committees must be in secret unless the subcommittee decided otherwise, which made it very difficult for a subcommittee to meet other than in secret. When tve opposed that suggestion we were promptly voted down; the old steam-roller was brought out and put in gear, and we were run over by the government majority on the committee. At the time it seemed to me a strange way to do business in a committee which was supposed to be entirely non-partisan, working as a group of individual members. As a matter of fact, I believe the evidence brought out before the subcommittees has indicated that most of these meetings need not have been held in secret at all; that no harm would have been done if the press had been present, and that, in fact, much good might have resulted if this had been done. That is particularly so because the subcommittees are dealing with specified subjects. If they had been going into particular departments in detail, there might have been more justification for secret meetings, but that was not the situation. For example, take the question of contracts with civilian flying clubs, associations or companies, which was dealt with by No. 1 subcommittee; or take other matters, such as food supplies for the forces, the inspection thereof, catering and salvaging of waste, and the construction of army and navy buildings, which were referred to subcommittee No. 2. In my opinion there was no reason why the meetings dealing with those subjects should not have been quite open.
In any event, it took the subcommittees some time to get started, and they hurried through their work. Perhaps No. 3 subcommittee had many more meetings than the other two; but if hon. members will refer to the reports of these committees they will see through them all a tendency to pull punches. The subcommittees are not hitting out at things that should be hit out at; all the way through they have pulled their punches. For example, look at the report of No. 3 subcommittee, which was dealing with headquarters organizations. At page 459 we find these words:
The subcommittee is strongly of the opinion that .a further careful study of adequate controls of army, navy and air force expenditures should be made immediately dn the belief that such controls will result in very large economies throughout the services, greater no doubt in some than in others.
The fact was, Mr. Speaker, that these greater economies could be effected in the air service; but rather than come out and call a spade a spade, the subcommittee said that all departments should be looked into, but that greater savings might be made in some than

War Expenditures Committee-Report
in others. Then, if we turn to page 452, we find the report of subcommittee No. 2 dealing with the inspection and1 marking of beef. It was reported to us that a certain system of marking had been inaugurated in Ontario and Quebec, and some members of the general committee said, "Well, why not recommend that this system be adopted in the rest of Canada?" The answer was, "Oh, no. We must not go that far. We might antagonize the quartermaster-general or somebody else. Instead of that we will put in these words," and they will be found in the report of the committee:
The quartermaster-general informed the subcommittee that consideration is being given to the extension of this practice throughout Canada.
There was a failure to face the facts and make a definite recommendation, which this committee should have done. We are the people who should have made the recommendation; we do' not have to stand back, to pussy-foot around and be afraid of criticizing higher officials, or of making suggestions that may not please those officials. If the committee is to be of any use, then it must make forthright suggestions on these questions.
In the report of subcommittee No. 1-and it is to that report I object most-we find that the subcommittee have dealt with contracts with civilian flying clubs, associations or companies. In their report they deal first of all with elementary flying training schools, and they discuss the question of these schools fairly fully. There were certain facts they did not have, such as the question of common shares, to which the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) referred this afternoon.
But, then, when they come to a discussion of air observer schools, we find this statement in the report, as it appears at page 451 of Votes and Proceedings-.
The subcommittee has not completed its inquiry as to operation costs and profits with respect to air observer schools. A conference has been called of executive officers of all of these schools to discuss operating costs and profits and the subcommittee is not prepared to make any report in regard to these schools until its inquiry in this regard is completed.
The inquiry with regard to elementary training schools had not been completed, either, but a report was made upon them. In committee of the whole we were told that with respect to air observer schools, profits running from 40 per cent to over 50 per cent were made in cases by these private companies. Some of us took the stand that that information should be included in the report to parliament; that parliament and the Canadian people were
entitled- to know that fact. Instead, this subcommittee decided that they would call into conference the officials of these air observer schools, and that they would try to beat them down in their profit, try to make a better bargain for the government-and, of course, try to make the picture look better. That was not the function of that subcommitee, n-or was it the function of the whole committee. It is not the object of this committee to go out and- make deals with contractors or with private firms. That is a job for the government. Yet, when we asked that the report of subcommittee No. 1 be referred back to them in order that they might obtain further information, we were again voted down on a strictly party basis.
Mr. GOLDING; And only two voted for that.

No; there were four. We
were voted down on a strictly party basis. In other words-
Mr. GOLDING; There were two.

The hon. member can make his speech later. In other words, the old steam-roller was brought out against us again. That amounts to soothing parliament and to soothing the Canadian people, and I say that this soothing combined with the secrecy of the subcommittee meetings, is dangerous to the nation at this time. If changes are not made, this war expenditures committee may do more harm than good. It may be a case of hindering, rather than aiding Canada's war effort.
It is now suggested that the committee should carry on during this summer. The suggestion is that it carry on- again as a committee of twenty-four members, presumably to continue sitting in secret. That would continue all summer, perhaps during four months, and there would be no house to which to report. What is the sense of anything like that? Where is all this to lead us? The Canadian people will think, "Oh, we are reasonably safe; there is a committee in Ottawa checking all these items of expenditure." Yet there is no way of getting the information from that committee to the public, and I point out that on the committee members in opposition groups are not in a position to have their proper share in the decisions made by the committee.
If the suggestion is adopted, the committee will continue to be one-sided. It will consist of eighteen government supporters, and six supporters of opposition groups. Just to illustrate the attitude and the frame of mind: When we were holding our last meeting, and discussing the report which would be brought
3750	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
in, the suggestion was made that the number of members on the committee be cut down for the work during the summer. I believe it was suggested that the committee should consist of fourteen members. There arose a discussion which lasted an hour or an hour and a half as to the impossibility of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec having different representation-from the government side, if you please!-on that committee.

On a question of privilege, the hon. member for Vancouver South has made a statement with regard to a discussion which he stated lasted an hour or an hour and a half, and which was a contest between Ontario and Quebec members-
I had not gone that far.

-as to the proposed
reduction in the numbers on the committee. I state definitely that that statement is false, and should be withdrawn. I state that on my responsibility as a member.

I do not withdraw it, because it is not false; it is true. There was argument that this province must have so many Liberals on the committee, and that province must have so many Liberals, and that they must have Liberals from every part of Canada -one from British Columbia, and so forth, and so forth. In the end they decided to increase the committee to seventeen, in order that there might be proper Liberal representation from the different provinces. That is not the way to fight a war. That is not the way for this committee to carry on. If it is to cariy on in that way, then its efforts will be useless, and the whole proceeding will be a farce.
I do not wish to condemn without suggesting a remedy. For that reason I suggest that if this committee is to sit during the summer, the number should be cut in half. That is, it should be cut from twenty-four to twrelve members, and there should be equal division; that is, five members from the government side and five from the opposition parties, with the chairman and vice-chairman from the government group. That would give a total of seven government members to five in the opposition groups. I suggest that this business of sitting in secret should be at least greatly reduced. Meetings should be held in public, except in those instances where public meetings would give aid to the enemy. In such event they should be kept secret.
Even then, the committee could not be expected to do as good work as the British *committee has done because, as I have said, the Canadian parliament is carrying on along strictly party lines, and because we started so
;
much later. The committee, however, would have far more chance of succeeding than it has had to date, and I believe it might be able to do a great deal of good for this nation in these very trying times.

Mr. Speaker, before attempting to tell the story as to the ground covered by the subcommittee on which I acted- as chairman, I think it only right that I should answer one or two of the observations of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). In the first place he stated that both the general committee and the subcommittees were dominated by party politics, and that they were overwhelmingly Liberal. He stated, and -repeated the statement several times, that the old steam-roller had been brought out and put into gear. I should like positively to assert that not only was the hon. member wrong and incorrect in making that statement, but he himself did not attend the meetings of the committees enough to know whether or not there was any partisanship in their work. He would rush in and get his attendance and then rush off to another committee.

That is not correct. I missed quite a number of meetings because I had to attend the meetings of the pensions committee, but when my hon. friend says that I would rush in and then rush out, he is not telling the truth. The times when I said that the steam-roller was used, I was there and was rolled out.

I am not saying that my hon. friend had not perfectly good reasons for not attending the committee; he was spending most of his time in another important committee, the pensions committee. He had a perfect right to choose which committee he would attend; but having failed to attend with reasonable continuity the meetings of the war expenditures committee, I think it ill behooves him to make the statements which he has made with regard to that committee. The members of the war expenditures committee who attended the meetings devotedly and continuously caught the spirit of the committee and they functioned, not on partisanship or political lines, but just as this house expected them to. With regard to the charge that the committee divided on political lines. I may say that the very afternoon about which my hon. friend complains and on which he attended the committee, the committee divided nine to ten. Was that a division on political lines? More of the steam-roller, I suppose!

On what question did
the committee divide ten to nine?

War Expenditures Committee-Report
I think the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), being entirely unhampered by knowledge of this committee, had better not waste the time of the house.
I certainly shall not get any knowledge from the hon. member.

I come now to the second point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, that we were pulling our punches. He gave as an illustration that he was told the committee had been informed that there was some evidence that air observer school companies were earning profits of from 40 to 50 per cent. Once again he did not tell the whole story. In failing to tell the whole story, once again I say that deliberate misrepresentation has been made of the facts.
I ask that the hon. member withdraw the words "deliberate misrepresentation".

I would point out to hon. members that I cannot be the judge as to what one member says happened in committee and another hon. member denies. Hon. members must take the responsibility in stating what are alleged to be the facts. However, the expression "deliberate misrepresentation" should be withdrawn.

I gladly withdraw that
without reservation. I shall be pleased to present to the house the facts of what took place and leave it to the house to judge whether the matter was misrepresented. These are the facts. Subcommittee No. 1 was delegated three tasks: to inquire into the commercial operation of air observer schools, of elementary flying training schools and construction contracts. The committee was appointed on May 4 or May 5, and we headed into these questions as quickly as we could. But we have not been able to complete our work on any of them although we got along further with the elementary flying training schools than with any other subject. We made a reasonably complete interim report on that subject, but we told the main committee that we had not completed our investigation into air observer schools. Perhaps I was guilty of indiscretion in being too frank, but I told the committee that we had the evidence of one witness who gave figures that established profits ranging from 40 to 62 per cent. We also told the committee, however, that we had the evidence of only one witness; that we had no right to prejudge the case; that we should have an opportunity of hearing both sides of the question before turning in a definite report.
I think it will be readily seen how wise the committee was in coming to that conclusion and how unfortunate it would have been if we had reached a premature decision without hearing both sides of the case. What did we find? A conference was called of all the air observer schools across Canada to discuss the whole problem of operating costs and profits. The subcommittee found at that conference that the gentleman who had given evidence establishing profits of from 40 to 62 per cent was entirely in error, that the profits were not half of that amount. Where would we have been if we had not "pulled our punches"?

I rise to a point of order. I do not want to challenge the memory of the hon. gentleman, but this evidence was taken in camera. I think the hon. gentleman has considerably understated what the original evidence was, as well as what the subsequent evidence was.
Fortunately I have extracts of the evidence before me. The evidence given in connection with example No. 1-I shall refrain from giving the name of the school because this was given in camera-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member should refer to evidence taken in camera.
Each member of a committee which has held meetings in camera must himself decide whether he can use that evidence.

Under normal conditions I would not refer directly to any evidence given in camera, but the hon. member who preceded me has made the statement that profits in air observer schools ranged from 40 to 50 per cent and that the subcommittee had deliberately "pulled its punches". As a member of that subcommittee I cannot let that grossly incorrect statement go out to the people of this country without refuting it. I appreciate my responsibility as a member, but I should like to give sufficient evidence to refute entirely the statement which has been made. I am doing this in the interests of the morale of this country.

I rise to a point of order. The committee decided that the sessions of the subcommittees should be held in camera. I think that means that the evidence given before such committee must be regarded1 as privileged. If the rule is relaxed in respect of one statement, then the whole value of "in camera" sessions is gone. If it is permissible to refer to a statement of fact given in "in camera" sittings, then it would follow that
3752	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
statements of expressions of opinion given in camera might also be stated in this house. I suggest to Your Honour that the distinction should be this: If any evidence or any facts are available from a source other than statements made in camera, then such evidence or facts may be given in this house. But statements that are made in camera and expressions of opinion given in camera ought to be regarded as privileged. Otherwise the purpose of "in camera" sessions is completely defeated.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I make this observation. The incident which has just happened illustrates the point that some of us who were not able to support the idea of holding this committee were not incorrect, in that evidence which is given in camera should not be used outside in any shape or form whatsoever. Here we have had a piece of evidence given in camera referred to in this house. It is evident that if it is referred to in this house it will be referred to outside this house by individuals who think they may properly do so in matters of conversation with the general public. It renders the holding of committee work absolutely useless if sittings be held1 in camera because no reference should certainly be made to such proceedings.

Mr. Speaker, I would suggest, in view of the discussion which has taken place, that if the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), will withdraw the statement that he made with regard to 40 and 50 per cent profits, I am quite content to leave that part where it stands.

Mr. Speaker, on that point I was not quoting secret evidence. I was quoting statements made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), as chairman of the subcommittee when we sat as committee of the whole.
That was in camera also.
No.

The position of the Chair is this. Subcommittees were appointed, and they, in their discretion, decided to hold meetings in camera. Evidence was given at those meetings in camera, and any reference that might be made to that evidence by any member of the subcommittee must necessarily be on his own responsibility as a member of parliament. I cannot decide that question for him, nor do I think the Chair is entitled to decide as to what shall be said by a member of this house with regard to the proceedings in a committee of which he is a member. So far as the point of order is concerned, I again

repeat that hon. members speaking on this question who refer to proceedings of the subcommittees must do so entirely on their own responsibility as members of parliament.

May I ask the speaker a question? Who gave the authority for the issuing of common stock, and was any mention of it made in the agreements between the government and the flying clubs? How did the common stock come into existence, and how much was paid for it?

I am sorry that I cannot answer that question as fully as I would like to, because, as mentioned in the report, in the time at our disposal we have not had an opportunity to check the records of each of these elementary flying training school companies. We are told, however, that the preferred stock, the 5 per cent stock, was sold at par. We are told that, as to some of the companies, only ten $1 or no par value shares of common stock were issued. At any rate, as to all of them we are informed that the common stock is held in trust for the flying clubs and that no individual can make a dollar profit. I am sure that when the subcommittee has had an opportunity of fully investigating the whole set-up of these individual companies, it will make a full and complete report to the house. At the present time that is as far as I can go.
Your subcommittee have also recommended that a complete study should be made regard-

ing the profits which these elementary flying training schools earn for the benefit of the flying clubs. I do not think it is talking out of school to say that a majority of the committee feels that a ceiling should be placed upon the gross profit which should be made in that regard. But there is one other word which I should add as regards profits earned by the elementary flying training schools. At the time the schools w-ere organized it was anticipated that each school would be able to train forty-eight pupils at a time. Through increased efficiency of the schools it has been possible to increase pupil intake to eighty, with the result that the flying clubs through their training companies have come along voluntarily and have asked that their per flying hour profits should be reduced from 50 to 25 cents.
When was that voluntary offer made?
It was made a little while after the committee began to function. I could not tell offhand the exact date.
May 1 ask the hon. member if the profits are subject to taxation?

I do not know. All I can say in reply to that question is, that the contracts provide that all these profits, other than the payment of the 5 per cent on the preferred shares, are to be kept in a reserve fund, invested in the main in non-interest bearing Dominion of Canada bonds, and none of them can be paid out during the duration of the contract, which is the duration of the war.
The essence of the contract, when one studies the whole picture, is simply this. No private individual can make any profit at all. The profit accruing to the clubs is held in the form of dominion bonds without interest; in other words, the essence of the transaction is that there is a future promise to pay from the dominion to these clubs when the war is over.
As to the work of the clubs, the evidence given shows without exception that they have carried on in an extremely efficient manner, both as to the training of pupils and with regard to the cost of operation. The house will be interested to know that their casualties have been extremely low. With a total of over 17-360 million miles flown, the elementary flying training schools have had less than one casualty per million miles-and perhaps that part of the training is the most hazardous to the pilot because it is during that part of his training that the raw recruit is doing his first solo flying.

War Expenditures Committee-Report
In conclusion, I might make a few remarks with regard to taxation. Taxation in this country has reached the highest level we have ever before experienced, and consequently the public are becoming extremely critical of expenditures. That is as it should be. I am pleased that this government has adopted, in so far as it is humanly possible, the policy of paying for the war as we go. High taxation not only benefits the country, in the sense that we are able to pay as we go, but has a restraining influence on any type of extravagance, and I am sure that as members of this house we all welcome the critical attitude of the public towards war expenditures, because it will lead to greater care being taken and it will have a restraining effect on anyone who might be tempted to try to profit by war work.
Then there is the final result that overshadows all these points, which is the fact that heavy taxation curtails present consumer demand for goods. When one reflects that the maximum capacity of any country to contribute to war effort (outside man-power) is the difference between total goods produced and the goods consumed, he can see how important it is that we should restrain present consumption. In that regard there is the final chapter, the position of Canada when the war is over. In every way in which we deny ourselves now, in every way in which we economize now, we are building up a vast reservoir of future consumer demand which will help to start the wheels of industry turning when the war is over.
I could not resume my seat without paying tribute to the other members of subcommittee No. 1 who sat with us in the work. That committee's work was done by two Conservatives and three Liberals. There was no partisanship visible or active in any way in connection with the work of that committee, and while we had a difficult problem to study, we reached a unanimous report. I wish to express my personal appreciation of the cooperation which was given by every member of the committee.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. J. T. Thorson (Selkirk) that the third report of the special committee on war expenditures presented to the house on June 4 be now concurred in.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, this afternoon when I asked the hon. member for Ilalton (Mr. Cleaver) a question, he suggested that I should not take up the time of the house because I was not a member of the committee and therefore could not know very much about its work. The lack of knowledge of what the committee did or tried to do is the principal reason for my rising to-night to protest against concurrence in the report presented by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson). When this committee was suggested I considered, as did other hon. members of this house, that such a committee could do a great deal of good work; that it might go a long way toward bringing about economy in our war effort; that as a result we might put an end to many of the extravagances which we knew were being committed; and that their findings, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr.' Diefen-baker) and the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said, would cause others to be careful in their work in connection with our war effort. Then we were told what would be the set-up of the committee; and instead of a committee which would do what we had visualized, I saw that it was to be a committee with an overwhelming number of government members. Why the change was made from fifteen to twenty-four members, I do not know, but it seemed quite plain that this larger committee would not bring about any better geographical representation, and therefore it could only be that the government wanted so many more of its supporters on the committee.
In my opinion, from the very start the committee was handcuffed and hobbled, and. in addition, its members were to be pledged to secrecy. Certainly it could not accomplish what it should be able to do if it were pledged to secrecy, because most of its findings would also be kept secret. Further, it was suggested that if any wrongdoing should be found, that wrongdoing should not
3756	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
be reported to the house or given to the public but should be told the government or the minister in charge privately, and the minister would see to it that appropriate action was taken. What that action might be, we would not know. Then all this committee was to do was make representations, which recommendations might be brought before this house, if it were in session, or before the responsible ministers.
I have closely followed the work of this committee and have read all available reports. In the beginning there was a long delay; it took weeks before the committee got under way and began to work on any plan. What have they done? In my opinion nothing has been done by this committee that should not have been done by the ministers and deputy ministers of the various departments. All the recommendations that have been made have to do with the internal economy of the various departments. The committee has found that there are men in the Department of National Defence and other war departments, some of them high-ranking officers, who are receiving pay and allowances for doing work that a clerk could do, and that as a result there is a tremendous unnecessary overhead. Surely we did not need a committee of twenty-four members of the House of Commons to set up an efficient system within the offices of the Department of National Defence. I realize that the ministers are busy, and cannot give to these matters of internal economy within their departments the attention a man in a private business might be able to give. But the ministers have deputies for all these departments. They have administrators, and if those men are not able to set up proper and efficient systems within those departments, then they are not fit to hold their jobs as deputy ministers.
There is no business in Canada which could operate on the basis on which some of these government departments operate, and it is about time we began to realize that fact. We have increased by many thousands our civil service staffs. We have increased their pay by hundreds of thousands of dollars. The Canadian people know that. Every now and again an article appears in some newspaper with respect to the money paid to people who are working for the government. I have applications every day from people who want to work for it and, to my mind, too many who wanted to work for the government got their chance to work for it, with the resultant inefficiency and heavy overhead in some departments. Why should it take a committee of twenty-four members to find a lack of efficiency in a department of government?

The committee also investigated other branches of the service, and they have made certain recommendations in that regard. I have in mind particularly the air training plan. This afternoon an insinuation was made -one which practically amounted to a charge- respecting the tremendous profits accruing to private air training schools. Even if the profit is half of what was suggested this afternoon, that is not a matter that should have to be the subject of investigation by a committee of twenty-four members of the house. Surely that, too, is a matter of internal economy within the Department of National Defence for Air. The men who negotiate and draw up the contracts for these air training schools should be in a position so to regulate and draw up the contracts that they could see to it that unfair profits were not made. We must make up our minds to the fact that whether in war time or in peace time there is always an element in the country who are desirous of making huge profits out of someone else's misery. Surely cases of this kind are purely matters with which departmental officials themselves should deal. It should not be necessary to set up a committee to decide such questions as these.
If the committees were permitted to sit during the recess, and continued to investigate only such matters as these, then certainly the people of Canada would be up in arms at the suggestion that it is going to cost $360 a day for the members alone, at the rate of $15 for each member, besides the costs of the staff, to investigate matters which ought to be the business of the minister and his deputy. Why do we need a committee to decide whether or not soldiers are getting cow beef or good steer beef? Surely those are matters for men within the department. The question of salvage in the various camps should be the business only of the men who are at the head of the camps. That is why they are put there. They are there because they are supposed to have the ability to run those camps; they are supposed to know how to handle these various matters.
Therefore I say that the people of Canada are not prepared to pay $15 a day to members of the House of Commons to delve into matters which should be the business only of the ministers and deputy ministers. The ministers should hold the deputy ministers responsible for the proper and efficient administration of these matters. I thought when this committee was set up it would investigate some of the things which had been done prior to the setting up of the committee. I thought it would look into some of the contracts which we knew were rather fantastic and extravagant

War Expenditures Committee-Report
-not to bring them to the light of day, but at least to see to it that any further contracts which were made would be made on a proper business basis, and see to it that we received a dollar's worth of value for every dollar expended.
I thought one of the matters which would have been referred to the committee would have been the Tilley report. That report is far more important than the people generally realize, or than the press would let them realize, because, when the Tilley report was presented, the press of this country came out with the statement that there was nothing much in it, and that there was nothing particularly wrong with the contract. We know there was; there was a great deal wrong with the contract. Do hon. members think the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) would have gone to Toronto to get Mr. Tilley, one of the most outstanding, if not the most outstanding, lawyer in this country, to investigate that contract, had there not been some reason for doing so? There must have been a reason for it. The reason was that it seemed as though the contract was running into huge sums of money, and the firm was making huge profits. That was generally rumoured round the country. The result was that Mr. Tilley was asked to investigate. He sent in his report, and if hon. members would read between the lines of that report they would get some idea of the extravagance of the contract made with the Acadia Construction Company. One realizes how perilously the whole matter was handled from the very start; one realizes the pressure the Acadia people put on. Then, when it seemed to the government that speed was so necessary, they signed the contract. After the contract was signed, the government found it had given one of the juiciest melons any construction company in this country ever got. If hon. members will read the report they will find that the company was in a position to charge rentals-

When it was brought to the attention of the late Hon. Norman Rogers, the then Minister of National Defence, by Mr. Vaughan, the minister wrote Mr. Vaughan and told him he was sorry that Mr. Vaughan did not like the terms of the contract, but that since it was signed, nothing could be

It is true that some of the extravagances which were apparent under this contract have now been cured, or at least I hope are in the process of being cured; but the contract has not yet been completed, settlement has not been made, and there are still points at issue.
If a committee is going to function on war expenditures, the government ought to see that this type of thing is investigated. Other contracts were given on a similar basis. Why is a man enabled to charge three days' rental in twenty-four hours and keep his machinery going continuously? Such a thing could never be done in private business, but that is what is happening in government business. It is contracts such as these that the people of this country expect this committee to investigate. This is the sort of thing we want investigated. We do not want scandal brought out. I have said on more than one occasion in this house that the worst thing that could happen to our war effort would be scandal. I am not suggesting it, nor do I wish to hear of it. But these are matters that ought to be investigated so that nothing of the like will occur again. Are there other contracts of a similar nature being performed by construction companies in this country for the government?
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) referred to the construction of a plant north of Winnipeg, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) said that it would be referred to this committee for investigation. Has it been referred to the committee? Has the committee dealt with it at all? Is it not more important to deal with that than with the question of whether cow beef is being fed to the soldiers? These are matters that we have to watch. These are the things that we thought the committee would delve into with the idea of seeing that no further contracts such as this would be made.
The committee asks the privilege of sitting during the recess. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has asked members of this house' to go out through their constituencies and do everything they possibly can to recruit men for the army or for the war services, to get men to go into the fighting forces of this country for SI.30 a day, or slightly more in the form of allowances if they are married. We are supposed to go out and ask young men to enlist, and yet we are sitting here to-day when a suggestion is made that we should endorse a motion to appoint a committee, the members of which will receive
3758	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
$15 a day each. I realize how difficult it must be for some hon. members to sit on such a committee; I appreciate the sacrifice that they would have to make!
There are many hon. members in this house who are specialists in certain lines of endeavour, and right from the outbreak of the war many of them have offered their services to the government, not for a dollar a year but for nothing. They were not asking for a living allowance. It is true that they received acknowledgments of their letters, but they never got a chance to do anything. Members of this house feel frustrated; they feel they are not able to do the things they would like to do. I realize how difficult it would be for some hon. members to sit on this committee without receiving some allowance, and I think it would be quite proper to pay them actual out-of-pocket expenses. When we are asking men to enlist in the army; when we are asking the people to dig deep in their pockets for the war loan; when we are asking working men and women who are not getting extravagant wages to contribute to war services and to buy war savings stamps, it is not right for us to pass a motion which will provide $15 a day to hon. members for sitting on a committee between sessions.
A member of the House of Commons receives an indemnity of $4,000 a year. If the house sat for the whole twelve months, that is all he would get; that is all he would be entitled to. He would have to make that sacrifice. When a member accepts a nomination to run for a seat in the House of Commons he knows what he is going to get and he knows what his responsibilities will be. If there are men in this house who should sit on this committee because of their particular abilities, who feel that they can do a real job, they should not expect to get $15 a day over and above their indemnities. I am opposed to this committee sitting unless it can do more work than it has done already, unless it can do some real work, and I am definitely opposed to the members receiving $15 a day each.

In committees the first thing to understand and to keep clearly in mind is the order of reference. The inquiry by the committee must conform to the order of reference. The order of reference to the war expenditures committee was agreed to by both parties, and the chairman of the committee started the investigation according to the order of reference. He called in deputy ministers and high officials of every department concerned. For the first month, if members recall well, the committee held its inquiry in open sessions and proceeded-
. . . with a general review of the manner in which the Department of Munitions and Supply functions as a central purchasing agency for the three departments of National Defence, army, navy and air, from the time it receives a requisition or contract demand from one of such departments until such requisition is filled, of the various types of contracts which are entered into by the department and the bases upon which such contracts are let, of the various checks and controls in the matter of cost accounting that are exercised, of the manner in which the purchasing organization within the department is set up and functions and a general exploration of the existing checks, controls, care and supervision in the matter of procurring necessary munitions and supplies.
This was the basis of our further inquiries and for the appointment of subcommittees. If this was not the correct procedure to follow, I wonder why the members of the opposition who were sitting in that committee did not object at the time. They all agreed that the procedure was the necessary one so that members would receive correct information. I recall at the first meetings we discussed the munitions and supply act. Many of the members did not know exactly the contents of the act, and before proceeding further it was certainly logical to make themselves acquainted with the different sections and provisions of the act. This lasted for about a month until the Easter recess, and then three subcommittees were appointed and went to work, sitting in camera. This was also decided by the committee of the whole, that the subcommittees would sit in camera unless they themselves decided to sit in the open. Two subcommittees sat in camera and one in the open. At the end of their sittings it was recommended-and this is mentioned in the third report of the committee:
That the minutes of proceedings and evidence of such meetings of subcommittee No. 2, referred to in your committee's second report as were not held in camera, be printed, 500 copies in English and 200 copies in French and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.
These committees two weeks ago presented reports to the whole committee. These three reports were adopted by the committee, and they form part of the report of the whole committee.
3760	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
When the war expenditures committee was appointed, certain reasons were given for its appointment. These reasons were given also by the hon. leader of the opposition. If hon. members will read carefully his speech and the other speeches by members who spoke on the appointment of the committee, they will find that the arguments in favour of the appointment of such a committee were: first, to assist the government in effecting economies and avoiding waste; second, a similar British committee had had good results in Britain; third, to enable private members to perform a patriotic duty; fourth, that the representatives of the taxpayers could get information as to how the taxpayers' money was being spent; and lastly, to satisfy the people that we are doing all we can to get value for the money rve spend.
During all the sittings of the committee and of the subcommittees I believe every member had in mind these purposes when examining the witnesses who came before the committee or subcommittees. I may state as a member of the committee that all went well until the last meetings of the whole committee, but at these last meetings the members of the opposition started to find fault with the procedure that had been followed. I do not blame them. They started saying that this committee could not function because there were too many Grits on it and not enough Tories. The hon. member who represented the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation stated that he was satisfied. The hon. member associated with the Social Credit group was not there at the, time. Hon. members who criticize in this fashion seem to forget that we have had special committees of this house in years gone by. In 1932, when there was a special committee on civil service matters, although the Liberal opposition numbered eight-one or eighty-two members, we had only two representatives on that committee, the present Mr. Justice Chevrier and Mr. Vallance. I recall that Liberal members were far from satisfied in having so small a representation, but I suppose that it was according to the system and that we received the treatment which seemed fair to the government of the day. Later on, the price spreads committee was appointed, on which we had only four members. Again we were not satisfied; but, after all, the arrangement flows from the existing system of government.
After having listened to-day to the speeches of some hon. members, I am inclined to be discouraged at the manner in which democracy is treated in our own parliament. Hon. members criticize our way of proceeding with public matters; on the other hand, they are

all willing to fight for our present way of life. To my mind it seems contradictory that we should criticize everything the House of Commons does, and yet say to the people, "My goodness, this is all wrong, but just the same we are going to fight to uphold our institutions and our parliamentary procedures." I wonder whether hon. members who speak in this fashion reflect that they are doing, perhaps, more harm outside the house by speeches in this vein than the good they can accomplish by their work on the committee.
The hon member for Waterloo South was quite critical of the proposed $15 a day living allowance for members of this committee. I do not recall the amount of the allowance received by members of Mr. Stevens's price spreads committee.

speechtext:
Nobody criticized the amount at that time. The best argument for maintaining an allowance for hon. members who sit on committees is that there are many who cannot afford to attend unless they receive it. I believe that their constituents and the people of Canada generally expect hon. members to attend the sittings of the committee; they believe that their representatives can do a useful job for the country, and are willing that they receive a living allowance. Some suggestion has been made that hon. members should sit without receiving any allowance. That may be all very well for the millionaires, if any there be, who are members of the committee, but the state does not require that sacrifice from the ordinary man who has to come to Ottawa and maintain himself as well as, perhaps, his family here. All the state asks is that a member shall do the best he can for his country; it does not want him to starve while he is doing his duty. Some hon. members have assured me that they could not afford to remain on the committee unless they received some allowance. I am not interested in the amount, but I believe hon. members should receive something. It is not a question of hon. members being paid to do their duty. They will have made enough sacrifice in spending the summer months here, without being required to pay their expenses.
I do not share the idea of the hon. member who thinks we should reject an allowance. I shall have no hesitation in accepting my living expenses, and I believe my constituents will approve my doing so.

War Expenditures Committee-Report
They believe that what I can do here will be worth more than my living expenses. There will be no criticism across the river if I accept an allowance, just as there was no criticism when the Bennett government paid $20 a day to the members of the price spreads committee. Why should we be holier than the holy? It seems to me sometimes that some hon. members speak just for the press and to impress the public and show how good they are. If it were their obligation to come here and spend six months of their time without receiving any living allowance, how many would accept the job? I do not hear a very loud response.
If we are convinced that we can do useful work as members of the committee, that we can save the country money by reforming certain procedures or elements of the system, it will be worth while for the country to defray our living expenses. This committee was set up to try to find ways of saving the people's money if there is waste in war expenditures. I do not suppose that up to the present time any hon. member could make an exact estimate of possible economies, but I am sure nobody will say that the committee cannot find ways and means to save money. I have not yet heard one member of the committee assert that it is of no use. All its members, whether on the government or the opposition benches, believe that there was good reason for its appointment and that it can accomplish something useful. But some hon. members are determined to criticize. Having convinced the government that the committee should exist, they are now trying to find reasons to make it disappear. It is a funny world we live in. In one breath they advocate the committee; in the next breath they assert that everything the committee is doing is wrong. I believe, however, there is one thing upon which we all agree. The moment this motion is passed, it will be found that all our members, like good little boys, will come back here on July 2 and sit on the committee and do their best. They are all good citizens, sincere and ready to work, and most of what we have heard this afternoon was intended merely for the galleries or to put on a show, because the members who have criticized are as interested as we are in the welfare of our country, and they are doing useful work. I wish to state that the hon. member for Danforth, one of the prominent members of the committee, has been very helpful; he has offered a number of useful suggestions. I can say the same with regard to the hon. member for Lake Centre, a hardworking member, and also with regard to the hon. member for Vancouver South, whose only grudge against us is that he would like to have as many Conservatives on the committee as there are Liberals.

speechtext: But I am no less alarmed when I see this committee, mostly an organized crowd of lawyers, wanting to spend the summer here. I have every confidence in the government and in the way things are being handled, and I believe that a lot of the criticism can be cut out; I do not think it is necessary. subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT

Here the house has appointed a committee, and there is not a doctor or a dentist or a druggist on it. Yet there are many doctors in the house, and they should be represented on a committee dealing with medical matters; I would not care what parties they were taken from. The idea of having a medical committee without a doctor, or even a druggist or a dentist! A band of lawyers are going to deal with medical questions! On that subject I would not give five cents for the opinions of all the lawyers in the house. They do not know an osteopath from a chiropractor. One can talk to them about anything, and what do they know? They are simply quacks when they step out of their profession and express opinions in medicine. I have sat in committees and heard the most absurd statements made, and I have said to myself, "If this sort of thing should happen in a medical committee, heaven help Canada." I hope that these men will be sent home to employ themselves in other ways so as to allow the government to go ahead. They have only a nuisance value.
