subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext:
Before
making any general observations on the motion before the Chair, may I say first of all that after listening to the speeches that have been given to-day, I am wondering whether we realize the serious state in which our civilization finds itself at this moment. I wonder whether a good deal of the comment that has been made, both in the committees and in this chamber, might not profitably be relegated at least to a secondary position so that we might all fully realize, as was said over the air the other night, that the hun is at the gate, and that there is a war [DOT]on. Let us get down to business and see if we cannot in some way assist Canada, even if it must be through the instrumentality of a partisan government. If that is the only way we can do it, then let us go ahead and do it that w'ay. I say that, much as it annoys me to see evidences of partisanship displayed at this critical time.
In approaching the consideration of this third report and the motion for concurrence therein, I wish to place on record the reasons why as a member of the committee I find it necessary to vote against the report. I would refer to what the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) said just now. Not until within the last two or three weeks was there any dissension-I believe that was the word he used- or any conflict of opinion. Look at the record. At the very first meeting that was held, the result of the proceedings of the committee was adopted on division, and the reason for the division I will recite in a moment or two. Before doing so, however, and in order to make the record complete, I will read from the report to show what is asked for. I quote:
1.	That the committee continue its inquiry notwithstanding such adjournment.
2.	That the committee be empowered to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house and to adjourn from place to place; to sit in camera or otherwise as it may from time to time determine; to determine the manner and extent to which the evidence and proceedings should be printed or typed and to employ such secretarial, clerical and other assistance as it may deem necessary.
3.	That six members of the committee constitute a quorum during the said adjournment and that standing order 65 (3) be suspended in relation thereto.
4.	That any subcommittee appointed by the committee have power to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house and to adjourn from place to place.
5.	That the minutes of proceedings and evidence of such meetings of subcommittee No. 2, referred to in your committee's second report as were not held in camera, be printed, 500 copies in English and 200 copies in French and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.

Subcommittee No. 2, I may say in passing, was the one on which I had the honour to serve.
As I said a moment ago, at the very first meeting of the committee there was not unanimity of opinion as to the manner in which the committee should conduct itself; and after we had resolved among ourselves in this chamber that, as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has said, everything political should be left outside the committee room, we saw evidence at once that our friends who occupy the treasury benches were using the steam-roller, as an hon. member has said, to have their will imposed upon the committee.
I recall asking that the first report be one of the kind which is common in this house, namely, that the evidence be printed. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) insisted on a definition of policy, as to whether or not we should sit in open session. He was the first one to raise that question. I had the honour to move a motion in that committee-as a member of the committee and not as a member of any political party-that there be open sessions, but the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), did not put my motion. He endeavoured to discharge the committee that day without the question of open sessions being considered. He rose from his chair and adjourned the committee until the next day, or tried to adjourn the committee until the next day, without giving consideration to the item which has the first place on every report that I have ever seen presented to this house, namely, that the evidence be printed, 500 copies in. English and 200 in French. Then, when it was called to his attention, the secretary of the committee put a note on the record. They retired from the committee at one o'clock that day and returned the next day; and even though my motion was not put, the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) rose in his place, heading off the member for Danforth, and put the motion himself, when he saw the spot they were in, that the evidence must be printed. The motion was put and carried, and the report came down to the house, but that section of the report took its place fifth on the list instead of first, where it ordinarily belongs.
That responsibility is entirely that of the chairman of the committee in introducing that partisan feeling at the very start. But we were all, or most of us at any rate, imbued with the idea that we might be able to do something on behalf of the war effort, and we tried our level best throughout the sittings to ignore all such indications of partisanship.

War Expenditures Committee-Report
My second reason for voting against this general report is that we have not had the aggressive leadership within the committee which the people expect from it; that we have not applied ourselves with diligence to the work -which was entrusted to us; that we have not carried out the mandate of the Prime Minister, namely, that the private member was to have an opportunity to do something effective. In the United Kingdom a similar committee was set up in December, 1939. The idea was advanced in this house in December, 1940, one year later, and we did not get down to any particular work until March 12. That much time was lost. We had altogether nineteen sessions, and the three committees had thirty-four, an average of a little over eleven each. And we thought we had work to do.
On April 8 we adjourned for the Easter recess. Nothing was done from April 8 to April 30, and very little until May 5. Everything seemed to be operating in such a way as to discourage us from going ahead with the work; yet my hon. friend the chairman of the general committee in his opening speech, when the bid was made for the chairmanship of the committee, suggested that we should be realists on the committee. "Let us all be realists on this committee," he said. But I have seen no evidence of any desire on his part to be realistic in the committee. To-day he said that our principles were confused but that now they were being clarified. I would say that it is confusion worse confounded after the speeches which have been made to-day. Why do I say that? Because the chairman has surrounded us with all sorts of inhibitions with regard to the purposes we had in mind.
The Minister of Munitions 'and Supply (Mr. Howe), when asked a question earlier in the session, replied that this committee would be sitting shortly and could consider the point raised. To-day the minister rose in his place during the heat of argument and said to the hon. member for Lake Centre, "Make your charge." The chairman of the committee emphasized time and again that this was not a public accounts committee; yet to-day the Minister of Munitions and Supply says, "Make your charges." Then the hon. member for Selkirk went on to say that this was not a fact-finding committee. Someone asked, "What is it?", and I begin- to wonder what kind of committee it is. We seem to be making the rules as we go along; we do not seem to have any plan or policy with regard to the conduct of the affairs of the committee.
When the committee does sit, what do we find? I do not mind helping in some way on a general committee of this kind; but the
hon. member who has just resumed his seat said that we were privileged to have a great deal of legal talent on the committee. I would not say that this was political legal talent, put there for the purpose of seeing that nothing happened to the- administration; but after we convened, how often did the chairman of the committee ask the members of the opposition, "What do you want to do now?" or "What do you say to that?" or "Will this meet the situation?" There was not a constructive suggestion from any of the Liberal members of the' committee; the discussion centred round what those of the opposition wished to say. What did they want to investigate? We were not applying ourselves as a body of eighteen men who had left their politics on the doormat; we were placed in the position of asking questions at the behest of the chairman. Then, when the question was asked, we had to sit and listen to a lecture by the chairman. The hon. gentleman said that one of the advantages of having closed sessions would- be that hon. members would not make speeches, but I say to him that in all my experience with many committees and boards of one kind and another I have never seen a chairman who had so much to say, who gave so many lectures to the members of the committee, as he did during the course of the proceedings of this committee.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext: The hon. member had a lot to say, too.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext:
Had I not had a great deal to say, Mr. Speaker, there would not have been very much work accomplished, because the other members of the committee who were supposed to be working in the interests of Canada sat there dumb and had nothing to offer unless it was to talk down some constructive idea that had been advanced by one of the opposition members of the committee.
I have referred to the question of sitting in camera. In connection with this committee I am probably in a class by myself, since I am the only member of that committee who has not sat in camera at any time. I have been sitting in open session throughout, and if I am privileged to continue to serve on this committee I intend to continue to sit in open session. Why? The people of this country are kept informed by a censored press, which is very careful not to hurt Canada's war effort. I believe the work of a committee sitting openly will have a far better effect on Canada's war effort, from many points of view, than will the work of a committee sitting in camera, as to which the people of Canada can have no knowledge
3764	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
We must keep the morale of our people at a high level, and the only way that can. be done is by keeping them informed and taking them 100 per cent into our confidence. There is no hon. member who would make a single utterance that would give any comfort to the enemy. If there should be such a member, he does not belong here; he should be ostracized and compelled to find some other sanctuary.
Let Canada know the facts. Let the private serving in the ranks know that we are helping. Let the contractor who wants to obtain a government contract know that we are not only helping him but also watching him, in order to see that the contract is fair and right. Let the officers in our camps, who are looking after the men, know that we are anxious to help them, but that any extravagance on their part is going to be checked. Let them know how that is going to be done; let them be given a little guidance. Let the man working in a munitions plant know that we are helping in every way possible and that his boss is not making extravagant profits. Then the man will go to work in the morning with a little better feeling than will be the situation if he hears over the radio or sees in the press that a committee is sitting in secret to examine these matters. If the working man learns that we headed into many mare's-nests, to use the words of the hon. member for Halton, and stopped there without learning what else was in the nests or what was going to come out of them, does that inspire confidence in the government? Yet the hon. member sits in secret session at the behest of the chairman of the general committee.
This afternoon the hon. member for Halton let the cat a little way out of the bag in one or two respects, rather to our surprise. Then the minister who was leading the house at the time, the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) rose and slapped the hon. member gently on the wrist, telling him, "You must not do that; it is not quite right." The minister also appealed to the Speaker for support, and he was reinforced by the chairman of the committee, who delivered a little lecture on ethics and gave the hon. member for Halton a verbal spanking. But after the last slap had been delivered, the hon. member rose in his place and in a split second gave his position mature consideration and intimated that he would say nothing more about it; but the mature consideration came after he had received his little spanking from his senior, the chairman of the committee, and the minister then in charge of the house.
The hon. member for Halton rather scolded the hon. member for Vancouver South for not 
having attended all the meetings of the committee. No man in this house has done more for the returned men of this country than has the hon. member for Vancouver South. I complained previously because this committee sat while the pensions committee was sitting. The hon. member for Vancouver South divided his time between the two committees as best he could, and was absent from the war expenditures committee only when something of importance was being considered by the pensions committee.
Some of the rest of us found ourselves in an awkward position. Personally, I was supposed to appear on three committees, as well as in the House of Commons. That was four places I was supposed to be in at the same time. I had sat on the committee on railways and shipping since its inception; but this session, because a more important committee was sitting, I found myself of necessity absenting myself from the railway committee. I did not miss one meeting of the war expenditures committee, but at the same time I had to carry along my other work. Then the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) rose in his place, and asked permission to have the committee on banking and commerce sit while the house was sitting. Then, in addition, the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines was sitting while the war expenditures committee was sitting. We were supposed to be in five places at one time. It is rather bad form for the hon. member for Halton to criticize the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) for missing the odd committee.
Then, after the demonstration to-day by the hon. member for Halton, it runs through my mind to ask what confidence the witnesses who are called in future to attend camera sittings will have, if they realize that the matters discussed in those sittings are to be discussed openly in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Halton has said either too much or too little. He has crippled our activity so far in carrying on a discussion of that subject, and not giving the whole thing. We wonder what really happened in the secret committee, and whether or not we shall find out. I do not know whether we shall ever find out exactly what happened.
Inasmuch, however, as I had the honour to serve on subcommittee No. 2, and inasmuch as that subcommittee was favoured with a chairman who took a fairly broad view of things and who kept the sessions wide open, perhaps I might confine my remarks to what occurred in that particular subcommittee. The sessions were open, and I congratulate the chairman of that subcommittee, the hon.

War Expenditures Committee-Report
member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) for keeping them open. I say to him and to the house that if his committee is reconvened it should be kept wide open.
Incidentally, we were all prematurely fired, as it were, or dismissed.	But if we get
together, and re-form ourselves, and if the hon. member is again honoured with the chairmanship of the committee, then let him keep the same broad, open view he has had with regard to the conduct of the affairs of that committee, and he may make some progress. Further, I say to him, and this in a critical tone, that when the chairman of the subcommittee drafts his report, and when he takes it to the chairman of the general committee, and they sit down to discuss the matter, he ought not to let the chairman of the general committee mutilate or destroy the original report from the subcommittee. I sat on a committee which passed a report of thirteen pages, and when we came back next day we found that the draft was mutilated. It was almost, in fact, destroyed. Only a few lines which the house now has before it remain of our report. Some of the vitals of that report were entirely removed from the animal, and he could not function. He was ruined, and much spoiled as a scarecrow-he had lost his scarecrow value.
The hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia (Mr. Mayhew) made the suggestion that it is impossible to cover the wide range the committee would have to cover. But the committee might be of some use on account of its scarecrow value. It might keep the crows out of the corn patch-the crows being those who would like to feed on the moneys available for war expenditures, moneys they are not putting up out of their own pockets. They would feed, even as the crow in the corn patch. If a scarecrow for each committee is going to be of any use, then I say to the general chairman, take that scarecrow out of the bam, put him up in the centre of the field, and keep the crows out of the corn patch. If any of the crows do get into the corn patch, I say that this house ought to realize the fact, as I said in my opening remarks, that these are serious times, and that what is now taking place is a very grim business. We ought to put that crow up against the wall, and shoot him. That is the way I feel about this procedure, and that is what I would do with those who would get into the corn patch to profit on war expenditures.
Therefore I criticize the hon. member for Swift Current most vigorously for permitting the mutilation of his report. And I am not alone. I call to witness the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone). He picked
up apples at Lansdowne park and looked at them. He put some in his pockets, and brought them up for the examination of experts in the house who knew something about apples. I have in mind the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rickard) who is not at present in his seat, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Mills) and the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Fraser). Any of those hon. members, or any hon. members who are not apple experts, but who know the difference between a domestic No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 and a cull, and who know the difference between fancy grade and domestic grade, must agree that some crow sold apples which were inferior to specifications, and had them delivered to Lansdowne park.
Why was the report mutilated? Why was that apple clause struck out? Some answer should be given. Just to keep the record straight I will read the specifications regarding raw apples. There are two general grades -and, in passing, why does the specification call for fancy apples in western Canada and domestic apples in eastern Canada? I believe the boys in the camps would be satisfied with good domestic apples, but why is there a distinction? I shall not take the time to read the specifications in detail, but the requirements for domestic apples state that the apples shall be Canadian grown, and at the time of delivery shall meet the requirements of domestic grade. The specification in the west, for fancy grade, is that the apples shall be Canadian grown, and at the time of delivery shall meet the requirements of fancy grade. I ask hon. members to rise in their places and say that the apples which they saw in these camps, and which we saw at Petawawa were either domestic or fancy grade -or were they just culls?
The hon. member for Waterloo South mentioned that we were talking so much about what kind of beef the troops are getting. I think we should know something about that matter, and I believe it would not do any harm to place on record some information as to what occurred. I get my information from a return which was asked for in the house by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) and the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin). They asked definite questions as to whether cow beef was being supplied in place of butcher steers. I point out these facts designedly to show that there seems to be a tendency on the part of the administration not to cover the whole field of an inquiry or to give a full answer to a question when it is asked in the house.
This return comes from the Department of the Secretary of State, and is signed by the
3763	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
Secretary of State (Mr. Casgrain). The return is dated Monday, March 31, 1941, and the questions are as follows:
1.	Was cow meat supplied in place of steer meat to military district No. 11 during 1940?
2.	If so, who was the contractor?
3.	For how many weeks was this meat delivered to military camps in British Columbia?
4.	Was quality of meat supplied up to department specifications?
The answer shows that on the afternoon of October 12, 1940-and I ask hon. members to note the date, because October 12, 1940, was a Saturday,-a contractor delivered a consignment of beef. The contract was to deliver such and so, according to specifications. The result was that a signed telegram was sent in these words:
Ration board rejected part shipment beef account wastage. Medical officer supports decision. Shipments cow beef this camp must stop. Matter being referred to headquarters.
At the same time another answer came down to a question which had been asked by an hon. member. He asked if the department had made a claim, and the answer was that they had made a claim and that $429 had been paid back in January, 1941. What else was paid back? Was there any voluntary contribution made to settle the claim? Is that the complete answer? If we could get a little more frankness, the answers might be worth while. Let me move to the next phase of this same question. What is cow beef? What are the specifications? Here are the specifications which were in effect prior to March 1, 1941, the old specifications:
Beef, fresh. The beef shall be butcher steer or heifers, both to be of good quality, properly fed, with suitable distribution of fat, and to be well slaughtered at least six days before the time of issue. The beef to consist of equal proportions of fore and hind quarters, the neck, head and offal to be excluded, and none of the suet to be withdrawn, the quarters to be standard dressing. The quarter of beef to weigh not less than 115 pounds nor over 185 pounds, or in cases where the demand is less than the weight of a quarter, it shall be supplied in one piece containing a fair proportion of best to other part. All beef must bear the official government inspection mark.
The new specifications, effective March 1, 1941, are as follows:
Beef, fresh.
1. Beef shall be from steers or young female cattle. Beef from bulls, stags, and mature cows and thin, underfinished or excessively fat carcasses, shall not be included.
What happened in the meantime; what happened in between the two sets of specifications, the old one demanding that it be heifers, and the new one demanding that it be young, female cows? I have a constructive

suggestion to make; otherwise I would not raise this question. In between comes the definition of what is required. I am going to put this on the record because I think it is a serious matter. Here is the letter:
H.Q. 1772-39-938 (DST>
Department of National Defence -Army-
Ottawa, Ontario,
7th February, 1941.
D.S.T. Letter No. 3-1941 The D.S. & T.O.,
All military districts.
Re: Specification for beef.
1.	As some misunderstanding appears to exist, as to the kind of beef that is acceptable under specification No. 7-M-4, dated 31st December, 1940, and in order to clarify the situation, it is desired that all R.C.A.S.C. officers i/c supplies be informed that maiden heifer or heifer beef is acceptable.
2.	The interpretation of heifer beef is a female animal which has calved once or twice but not more than twice, under these conditions the udder of such animals would be generally firm showing only a small percentage of sponginess. The acceptance of such beef will, of course, depend upon the carcass meeting all other clauses of the specification referred to in para. 1 above.
H. O. Lawson,
Colonel,
D. of S. and T.
It is absurd to ask officers in charge to tell whether or not the beef is cow beef or heifer beef. They cannot tell if it is a maiden heifer or whether she has had one calf or two calves, and they have no chance in the world to examine the udder. When the udder is taken off the carcase, it is shipped down to-the mink or fox farms to be fed.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext: My constructive-suggestion is that in the new specifications there should be a straight separation between the different kinds of beef.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext: The hon. member should read all the specifications instead of only half.

Here is the rest of it:
Beef shall be from relatively young animals, as indicated by a range from red to greyish colour in the spinal process and the ends of the vertebrae must show the soft pearl-like cartilages or buttons. The aitch bone will be red in colour and porous, having a pronounced knob at the lower end, and showing the presence of white cartilage. Beef shall be well fleshed with an exterior covering of fat over the loins and ribs which may or may not extend over the full surface of the chucks and rounds.
Heads shall be removed at the atlas or first cervical joint. Feet shall be removed by dissecting with a knife at the knee joint; front feet at the top of the radius; hind feet at the top of the tarsus. All protruding sinews shall i

War Expenditures Committee-Report
be removed. Carcases shall be split down the centre of the vertebrae and the spinal cord entirely removed. All bruises, blood clots and inflamed portions of the surfaces of the carcases shall be trimmed so that only the merest trace of the damage remains. Tails shall be removed at the second eocygeal or tail-bone joint. None of the suet shall be withdrawn.
Carcases shall be hung in cooler for six days prior to delivery. The beef shall not be beef that has at any time been frozen.
Quarters shall not weigh less than 125 pounds or more than 185 pounds, and shall be supplied in equal proportions of fores and hinds.
All beef shall bear the Canadian government inspection legend and shall be slaughtered in conformity with standard practices and according to methods and conditions approved by the health of animals division of the Department of Agriculture, Dominion of Canada, and the tenderer must state the establishment or establishments in which the beef he proposes to supply will be slaughtered.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that from that specification one could not lell the age of the beef?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext:
The minister
can reply when I have finished. I know a good deal more about butcher steers and heifers than perhaps the minister. I make this constructive suggestion. In future military beef contracts there should be a new inspection service whereby the government grader marks the beef in each plant with the letters "D.N.D.". I suggest that separate prices be requested for steers and heifers, and that they be invoiced in that way. This would be the fairest way to deal with the matter. The military people want beef that is not wasteful. In heavy, well-finished cattle, they claim there is too much kidney fat. There should be a better way of distributing these contracts, which in the end would benefit the farmer. If the buying committee could allot the contracts month by month, in accordance with the contractor's facilities to supply same, and on an agreed basis of quota, it would make for better conditions in the industry and assure a more uniform supply of beef to the military camps.
Under the present plan, if one packer secures a large share of the beef business at below market value, he is in a position to reduce the price to the farmer on this type of beef, or he may skimp on the quality he delivers to the camp in order to avoid a loss. The government do not want to buy beef on a basis that will mean a reduced price to the farmer. It should be as important to the government to take steps to see that a fair price is paid to the farmer for cattle supplied on military contracts, as it is to see that a fair price is paid for hogs and wheat. Why did the hon. member who is chairman of subcommittee No. 2 allow his report to be mutilated and changed? Instead of saying
that the beef supplied is stamped with "D.N.D.", why could he not be frank in his report and say that that which had been supplied previously, at least up until the last few weeks, had not been stamped "D.N.D."? The chairman of the main committee has said that individual members could not be allowed to take any credit to themselves for any particular feature of the work. In reply to that I would say that this committee ought to justify its existence by doing something of real value.
I shall discuss only one or two points in report No. 3. It might be all right to load up the inside service with civilians; there might be some economy there, but when it comes to the outside services and the camps, I am of opinion that all the men should be in uniform. At the present time there are too many civilians going into and coming out of the camps. Whether they are there for the good of the war effort or for their own good, I am not in position to judge. I would hesitate to allow a greater number of civilian personnel into the camps.
Subcommittee No. 3 made a few specific recommendations. They suggested that there should be a saving on stationery, printing, advertising, telegrams, telephones, transportation, heat, gas, oil and so forth. They might in the end get dollar for dollar value. The report in that respect alone has some scarecrow value. That little sentence alone will help. How much more helpful it would be if these meetings were wide open and the world knew what we were doing!
Another matter which concerns me greatly, and which I address myself to all alone, is the suggestion that the members of the committee receive pay while they are sitting during adjournment or recess, if we are going to sit. Speaking for myself, I say no. We are paid from session to session. That should be enough. I said in the committee, and I say to this house now, that for the duration of this war I shall be happy to serve anywhere. I shall be happy to serve at any war work at any time and do all I can to help out in our war effort in any capacity for the duration of the war. I am glad that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) is in his place to-night. I do not think I shall be breaking any confidence between him and myself if I remind him that at his telephonic request I arrived in Ottawa on October 15, 1940, and discussed with him some problems that he had on his mind in trying to check waste on behalf of Canada. At that time I had the honour and privilege of confirming our conversation, and
3768	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
the minister will recall that I wrote him a letter from Toronto which reads in part as follows:
October 22, 1940.
Hon. J. L. Ilsley,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:-
This will serve to confirm our telephonic conversation of Thursday, October 10th, the exchange of wires same date, and the interview given the writer in Ottawa, Tuesday, October 16th.
At this conference I intimated to you, in a like manner as I previously intimated to the Hon. Mr. Howe and the Hon. Mr. Ralston, that I am anxious to do everything possible to assist Canada in our war effort. I therefore place at the disposal of the government of Canada-
(a) My services as an individual to serve anywhere in any capacity.
I do not need to recite the other paragraphs because they cover just the matter of my giving the government material things over which I have some control. When I say to this house that I will not accept any remuneration whatsoever, I do not wish to tie other members of the house. Let their conscience be their guide so far as they are concerned. What matters if we do not win this war? That is the position we are in. In like manner I have also a copy here of a memorandum from one of the district recruiting officers, Toronto, as follows:
To District Recruiting Officer,
61 Albert street,
Toronto, Ontario.
Please interview the below-mentioned prospective soldier for enlistment in a branch of the Canadian Army (active).
Then particulars follow concerning the member for Danforth and his qualifications to be of some assistance in the ordnance department, signed by the recruiting officer for the district and myself.
While I am in this position, I will not under any circumstances accept any remuneration for any war work outside the ordinary sessional indemnity, and I intend to adhere to that course. Can we not realize, as the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Selkirk, said to-day, that these are grim days and this is a grim business we are in, and that we must have unity, we must have tolerance, we must not have speeches like that we had a minute or so ago from the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), ridiculing those of us who wish to serve. That gets us nowhere. We must have self-sacrifice. We must have a clear conception of the tasks that lie before us and start in to execute those tasks, let the chips fall where they will. Shoot the crows at sunrise. Make sure, Mr. Speaker, that 
every gun, every bit of ammunition, every tank, every ship, every plane, every man, and every dollar are placed at the disposal of democracy and used where democracy is fighting for its life. The front line of democracy to-day is in Britain, and let us help her in every possible way we can to complete the job.
The night before last I was rather intrigued by the closing lines of a radio address by Mr. Farrell in the "Between Ourselves" series, over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's national network, and I shall delay the house long enough to read them because the sentiments expressed in these verses have moved me to make some of the remarks I have made to-night. Let us all say in the words of this verse:
For all we have and are,
For all our children's fate,
Stand up ,and take the war,
The Hun is at the gate!
Our world has passed away In wantonness o'erthrown,
There is nothing left to-day But steel and fire and stone!
Though all we knew depart,
The old Commandments stand:-
'In courage keep your heart,
In strength lift up your hand.'
Once more we hear the word That sickened earth of old:-
'No law except the Sword Unsheathed and uncontrolled.'
No easy hope or lies
Shall bring us to our goal-
I should like to repeat that top line, "No easy hope or lies shall bring us to our goal." Those easy hopers and wishful thinkers to my mind are worse than the fifth-columnists. No easy hope, for we are in a grim business. We have work to do:
No easy hope or lies Shall bring us to our goal,
But iron sacrifice Of body, will, and soul.
There is but one task for all-
One life for each to give.
What stands if Freedom fall?
Who dies if England lives?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext:
I am not going to attempt to follow the eloquence of the last speaker (Mr. Harris, Danforth), but I should like to touch on one or two of the points discussed this afternoon by the members of the opposition on the committee.
First of all, it was suggested that in setting up the committee we should have followed what was done in England where there was, it was said, equality of representation on the committee; or, in other words, as many

War Expenditures Committee-Report
members of the opposition group on the committee as members of the government. I have looked at the composition of the British committee and of our own committee, and I find that in the committee of this house, where we have 184 Liberals, there are eighteen Liberals on the committee; there are thirty-nine Conservatives in the house, and four Conservatives on the committee; there are ten of the New Democracy group in the house, and one member on the committee; there are eight members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in the house, and they also have one member on the committee. If we followed the suggestion that was made by members of the opposition we would have as many Conservatives as Liberals on the committee except for the chairman.
Mr. GREEN; If I might interrupt the hon. member, my suggestion on that point was that the total opposition strength in the committee should be the same as the government strength, with the exception of the chairman and vice-chairman. My suggestion was not that there should be as many Conservatives as Liberals.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT
speechtext:
But other members of the opposition did not suggest that.
Let me now go briefly over the composition of the British committee. In the British house there are 387 Conservatives, and eighteen Conservatives on the committee; fifty-four Liberals, including the National Liberals, in the house, and there are three on the committee; there are 162 Labour members in the house, and eleven on the committee, and there is one member, Mr. Edwards, whose party I could not ascertain. Therefore we here in Canada have approximately followed the plan that was followed in England of representation by parties. If we look at the numerical strength of their parties, it will be seen that we have followed just about the same plan in the composition of our committee.
If we follow the reasoning of the opposition, we are required to assume that because a man happens to be a Liberal member of this house, there is something about him which disqualifies him from serving on a committee. This, it seems, is because the people of Canada happened to elect a large number of Liberals. After all, it was not the Conservatives who elected the Liberals; they were placed here by the people of Canada, and it is hard to understand why, because they happen to be members of a majority group, they cannot fulfil their duties or exert the privilege they have of serving the country on this committee. Such an argument altogether offends one's sense of fairness; for, after all, what can

be fairer than to give hon. members the right to serve in the proportion that the people have elected them to this house?
A word about the subcommittees. It has been suggested that in the old country their composition is so balanced that there cannot be any partisanship or any flavour of politics about the membership. Let us see how they are composed. There are eight subcommittees, and with your kind permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall briefly indicate their composition:
Coordinating subcommittee:	five Conservatives, one Labour,	one Liberal,	one
National Liberal.
Army	services:	five	Conservatives,	one
Labour.
Naval	service:	three	Conservatives,	one
National Labour, one Liberal, one, I think, a Socialist.
Air services:	three Conservatives, two
Labour.
Supply sendees: four Conservatives, one National Labour, one Labour.
Home	defence:	three	Conservatives,	two
Labour, one Liberal.
Trade, agriculture and economic warfare: three Conservatives, one Liberal Nationalist; one Labour.
Transport: four Conservatives, two Labour.
I find there no attempt to balance the membership of either the large committee or the subcommittees. Such a matter was never thought of over there. Members of the British parliament are given credit for having enough sense of fairness and justice to give impartial consideration to any and all matters when they are appointed to these committees. I do not take kindly the suggestion that because an hon. member happens to be a member of this group or that, he cannot give of his best in the present struggle and in our attempt to save every dollar and to see that a dollar's worth of service is given where a dollar is spent.
The next suggestion made by the opposition is that the proceedings of our committees should be open. They do not go to the British system to find arguments for that contention. In point of fact we go farther in this direction than they do in England. Opposition members in particular have been arguing that, because these committees operate in secret, there is something about them which should be looked upon with suspicion. Let me read a resolution passed by our main- Canadian-committee.	The wording is
important:
That the sittings of the subcommittee shall be in camera except as the subcommittee may otherwise from time to time determine.

3770	COMMONS
War Expenditures Committee-Report
I hold in my hand the report of the select committee for the sessions 1940-41 of the British parliament. It happens to be their fifteenth report, and at page 7 is this statement:
The subcommittee shall sit in private.
There is no provision whereby the English committee can sit openly from time to time if they so decide. Subcommittees there have not the power to hold an open meeting. It is a strange kind of argument which we heard, for example, from the last speaker, who said that he attended a number of committee meetings and that they were open, while the opposition speaker just before him argued that their party cannot continue to cooperate in this movement for efficiency of expenditures because the committees are meeting in camera. One contradicts the other. The committees and the subcommittees have the power to hold open meetings when they believe that the public welfare or the general good will be enhanced by so doing. There is no such power in the old country.
Let not the people of Canada be deceived by the notion that there is something suspicious about secret meetings of committees, that the members who serve on these committees have ulterior motives, that they have done something which should not have been done. Such conclusions are entirely wrong. We hear from the opposition that we should follow the English lead; the leader of the opposition himself (Mr. Hanson) suggested that these committees should adopt the English plan. Yet, when we follow that plan, and go even a step farther, we are accused of "muffling" practices, of doing things which should not be done, of standing for things which should not be tolerated.
Another criticism which rather disgusted me was the suggestion that steam-rollers were brought in and put into high gear. One might think that this committee was building highways. or crushing stone or something of that kind. Reference was made to "political pressure". It is my conviction, recalling the speeches of opposition members to-day, that I have heard more talk of politics and partisanship in this committee from speakers in half an hour to-day than I heard in the month I served on the committee. It is my recollection, and I give it as such, that the only member who indulged in any partisan talk on the committee was the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who obtruded it on several occasions. At no time did I hear any Liberal member mention politics. I can say the same for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and Social Credit representatives-the more credit to them.

Therefore, looking at this picture, I hope the country will not get the impression that there was a "scrap", as one hon. member remarked this afternoon. I have never attended a more friendly committee than the subcommittee upon which I served. We never took a vote; we never disagreed. There were two Conservatives and three Liberals, and we got along beautifully. I believe the same can be truly said of all the subcommittees. Contrary to the impression which has been spread here to-day that there was a lot of confusion and "scrapping", it is my recollection, which I am giving because I do not want the wrong impression to go out, that nothing of the sort took place.
It is unfortunate that the situation which exists now should have arisen. Suppose we go back a few months to the time when the leader of the opposition suggested the setting up of this committee. He gave as his reason the fact that expenditures made by the government bad to Be watched in the interest of the public. But what do we find now. One member after another of the opposition rises in his place and, for one reason or another, objects to the motion before the house being adopted, thus virtually breaking down the very fabric on which the committee is to carry on. One suggests that it should split up into territorial committees; another says that we should reduce the number; another says that we are not going at it in the right way; another says that it is too partisan; another says that there is not sufficient aggressiveness. Take all these and other representations that have been made, and you cannot come to any otheT conclusion than that they do not want the committee to carry on as it is. I give that as my frank understanding and impression.
Let us see what has happened. The leader of the opposition said that there were a good many expenditures, that a great deal of money was being spent and that a committee should be appointed. Very well; the government agrees. But what do we find to-day? They want the committee stopped. I say to the Canadian people that that is a good omen of what is happening in the departments if the purpose of the appointment of the committee, as was originally intended, is being made effective; that is to say, if they have to take the stand that expenditures have been fair, that there has been no extravagance or waste, then there is nothing further for the committee to do and their attitude can be understood. If they do not take that attitude, then they must adopt the alternative, which I cannot think they are prepared to adopt- that is, that they do not want to see economy in expenditures made.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
I suggest to the opposition that they should close their ranks. Let them consider the suggestion their own leader made. Let them reflect that this is a creation of their own party, which came about just because they suggested it; and instead of one member of the opposition offering one criticism and someone else another criticism, let them close their ranks. Let them be of one mind. There is no place in Canada at the present time in which anyone can serve to greater advantage in the war effort than on this committee, and I hope that the members of the opposition, when they think of what has happened to-day, will see the light to-morrow, will see where their privileges and responsibilities are, and will see fit to continue the committee as it is at the present time.
Shall the motion carry?

EXTENStON TO FARMERS WHO MOVE FROM TOWNSHIP AT END OF CROP SEASON
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 95, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Vien in the chair.
On section 1-Computation of sum awarded as assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Subsection 2 reads:
In an emergency year the minister may, subject as in this act provided, award to each farmer resident at November first of such year. . . .
That would mean that if he came four or five days before, he would be resident on that day. I wish to move an amendment that subsection 2 of section 1 be amended by substituting the words "resident from May first to November first of such year" for the words "resident at November first of such year".

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I move accordingly.

Will the minister explain a point which has arisen in two or three cases? I have knowledge of one in particular. Someone was farming and left the farm on October 19. In this case it was a woman, and she was married on that date and apparently was cut off from the bonus because it' 14873-2381
was held that she did not qualify legally. Under this, what would be the interpretation? Would the farmer have to remain from May 1 to November 1?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes; that would be the interpretation. As the act now stands, the farmer is required to be there on May 1 to qualify. This means that he will have to remain until November 1, all through the summer season, in order to qualify. As the regulations stand now, no date is set, and even if he were not there in January and his payment had not been made he would not be entitled to payment, according to the interpretation given by the Department of Justice recently. This fixes a date.
Suppose a man left in the middle of October when his year's work was done. He would not be eligible?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. He would not be eligible, but knowing that if he remained until November 1 he would be eligible he would, I should think, remain.

There is one matter which I think should be brought to the attention of the committee. This section as now amended will amount to a discrimination against any farmer who enlists for service in the present war at any time between May 1 and November 1. An exception should be made in that regard. During the past year several men wdiom I know completed their seeding operations and stayed on the farm during the summer. They did their threshing and enlisted, and they were denied the right to participate under this act, although they had contributed-as do all farmers-one per cent of the value of their several crops during the year.
Let me mention two examples. I have in my hand a letter dated May 6, 1941, from the prairie farm assistance branch at Regina ' regarding such a case. It is addressed to myself, and I am advised that a certain person has had his second payment of bonus denied him-"cancelled" is the word used-for the reason that he had discontinued farming, having joined his majesty's forces, and that the farm was not going to be operated in 1941 by any of his dependents.
The other case I have in mind is that of a young man of my constituency who enlisted in July, 1940, and, after service overseas, returned to Canada. He had his farming operations carried on, his harvesting and so forth after he enlisted and departed for overseas, but he has been denied this bonus. The reason given by the department is that since this young man enlisted in June, 1940 -which is an error-and was therefore absent
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

during the greater part of the 1940 crop season, he was ineligible for payment. I do not think any hon. member wishes to discriminate against those who, while engaged in farming, decide to enlist in the service of their country, and I suggest that an amendment to this section and to the next section should be made so as not to apply to those who enlist in the armed forces of the country.

I know of several cases similar to those mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre, which I was going to bring to the attention of the house, and therefore I am glad to support the suggestion advanced by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think it is scarcely proper to suggest that there has been or may be discrimination against those who have enlisted. If we were to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Lake Centre we would be discriminating in favour of the soldier, although I do not say we should not do so. The interpretation of the Department of Justice as to these provisions of the act, when cases of the kind mentioned were submitted to them, was to the effect that the act was intended to provide assistance to farmers in order to help them during the winter following a poor crop. That was said to be the principle underlying the act,-to make it possible for farmers to live on their farms until another crop had been put in; and I think in all fairness it should be said that this assistance was to be given for that purpose. But the Department of Justice say that since this is the principle of the act, any person who leaves the farm is not entitled to these payments under the act as it now exists, and they could not find any way of discriminating in favour of men who enlisted. We are now proceeding on the assumption that the man who has farmed all year, who has threshed and sold his crop, probably will be on his farm at least tinitil along well into October. After that, he just requires to remain on the farm until November 1 in order to qualify under this section.
I do not wish to do anything by way of legislation that would prevent any man from enlisting even for a month or fifteen days, but it is difficult to make any further provision than is contained in this bill. I do not think it would be any great hardship to those who are seeking to promote enlistments to say to these men, "You had better wait for *another two weeks after you have marketed your crop before you enlist." In any event I am told by those administering the act that their work would be made very difficult if we attempted to discriminate at all as between different groups. We do discriminate in behalf of the soldier to this extent. We say that if he

leaves any member of his family in charge of the farm, whether it be his brother, his father, his wife, or any immediate member of the family, we pay the bonus. Therefore there are several ways in which anyone anxious to enlist can obtain these payments, and I would rather hesitate to suggest that we should go further than we have gone, although I should like to see anyone enlist whenever he wished to do so. Probably by leaving the land under the direction of some member of the family they will be able to overcome this difficulty. There may be a few cases where people will not have relatives in the vicinity who can take over the direction of their farms. Perhaps those concerned will try to carry on their operations during the summer and enlist in the fall, which will permit them to receive their payments. Under this provision, if a man is on the farm as of November 1, he is entitled not only to the first but to the second payment as well.

I am glad that the hon. member for Lake Centre has brought up this question, and I was glad to hear the minister's reply. I have one or two of these cases which I was going to mention, but what has been said deals very well with the points I was going to raise. I have the case of one soldier who is having the work done on his farm by hired labour. He has no relatives in the vicinity; I think he went through the last war, and he has had to take back this land from the tenant who had it last year. What would happen in that case?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If he was back on the farm before May 1 he is entitled to the payment.
He is in the army now and cannot be back, but he is having the work done by a hired man.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Is it being done by a relative?
No; the man doing the work is married and living on the farm, but the owner is supplying all the machinery and paying all expenses. How about that case?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We probably would have to deal with a case of that kind under the new regulations defining a farmer or a person resident on the land. This man would not be a resident farmer under the present regulations, but it is possible the case could be handled by regulation.
I have the letter here. It is not worth while reading it, but that is the situation as briefly as I can state it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are so many different types of cases that I am sure they could

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
not all be covered by legislation. The whole administration of the act is along the line of doing everything possible within the terms of the act for men who are enlisting, but unless these men try to bring themselves within the terms of the act, the matter becomes rather difficult.

I am glad that this amendment is being brought in at this time. I have had occasion to discuss certain cases with the minister and the officials of his department. I intended to mention those cases at this time, but I find that unnecessary in view of this amendment. In view, however, of the injustices which have been caused in the past, and in order that they might be corrected, I would suggest that the amendment be made retroactive, and I would ask the minister to give that suggestion his consideration.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-Sum to be awarded in a crop failure area.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The same amendment is
being moved to this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I move accordingly.
Is there any increase in the amount payable in a crop failure area? I see the figure $2.50 mentioned here.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; there is no change; it is just the same.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Blocks ineligible for award.
Will the minister explain this section?

I am very glad to see this amendment, because we all know that a great deal of difficulty was experienced in obtaining the necessary resolutions substituting one piece of land for another. Municipal councils naturally do not like to take something out of the bonus area as well as they like to put something in it. I am glad that the minister has extended the provision so that under some circumstances a quarter of a township may be included, but I had rather hoped that when the amendment was brought down, a quarter of a township might have been the unit instead of depending upon the inclusion of other adjacent land within the area. I believe the closer we can get to the individual basis, the better it will be. During the
last several years, as the minister no doubt knows, practically all hon. members from the west have had brought to their attention cases of injustice or misfortune which could not be covered under the act, on account of the provisions of the act itself. When farmers are contributing to a fund which, many of them hope, will ultimately become a crop insurance fund, they are of the opinion with, I suggest, some reason, that when they make a contribution they should receive some benefit, if they are in a situation requiring aid.
Although this is a step in the right direction, I had hoped that the unit would have been made smaller this year, and that we might have got a little nearer to the individual basis. I know it is of no use now to suggest an amendment along those lines to the committee, but while I welcome the change in the act, one which I believe makes it fairer and better, still I hope that after another year's experience we may be able to get down to a unit smaller than the one provided under the present act.

I am more or less in agreement with this section. The minister knows a good deal about the difficulty there was last year in the area from which I come, and also in certain townships in his constituency. There was difficulty particularly in the townships, the south half of which were in the Qu'Appelle valley. I might say that it affected us particularly on the south side, owing to the good land which happened to be across the valley on the north side, in the minister's constituency. In that section last year they had a very good yield of from twenty to thirty bushels to the acre. That was the common yield immediately north of our district. Then, in the greater part of the valley, on the sandy land, they did not have a crop. As a matter of fact, they were below six or seven bushels to the acre, as the minister knows. I believe it is a fine thing that there is provision whereby these areas may be taken in so that they will be included in the bonus, if the yield is at a certain point. Therefore, with that part of the bill I am in accord.
There is one other matter I would bring to the attention of the minister. I would have been pleased to see an amendment to section 8 in the act, which would have eliminated1 the limit of 3,000 bushels. There were eases last year in two municipalities in my constituency where men had over 3,000 bushels, but they did not have any more than four or five bushels to the acre. Therefore I say that they were discriminated against. I suggest that if that section of the act were amended, so as to eliminate the provision for 3,000
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

bushels, it would be an improvement. There are many instances where that section serves to discriminate against producers. It so happened that some of these men had large areas, and had over 3,000 bushels. But it worked just the same where the yield was much less than 3,000 bushels. Has the minister given consideration to amending the act in the manner I have indicated?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We gave consideration
to the points raised by the hon. member, but the provision in the act was inserted just last year. It provides that any person with 3,000 bushels and an average crop in1 excess of eight bushels, is eliminated. Anyone with an average of eight bushels or under is taken in, though he has 3,000 bushels. Therefore there is provision for certain people who have low yield crops aggregating 3,000 bushels. That provision has been in only for one year. It is true that there were some hardships. Most of the complaints with which I had to do were cases which individuals could have corrected the situation had they seen fit to do so at the beginning. That is, these were family divisions which they claimed later on, and in connection with which no notification had been given in the early part of the season. Those cases could be rectified in some instances, but not in all. We thought it better to try out this provision for another year. The change now suggested will rectify most of the difficulty.

There is one further matter. I was wondering whether this year, in connection with inspection, the minister could work out a system whereby the same inspectors would do the work this year as did it last year. Last year we had a different inspector in our district from the one we had the year before, and he went over the territory in a different manner. I suggest that if a man is working in one territory year after year he would know the situation, and would become familiar with the farmers and their farms. The result would be that he would do his work more quickly and efficiently than a new man could do it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would suggest that
if hon. members have any objections, they might make them when we are discussing the estimates. Some of the points raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle might be more properly discussed under the estimates which I intend to call, immediately after this bill is passed. One item in my estimates has to do with prairie farm assistance expenditures. Matters such as inspection, methods of inspection, and everything of that kind might more properly be discussed under the estimates.
[Mr. Perley.3
That is satisfactory.

I was disappointed with section 7 in the act, as amended in 1940, on account of the strings attached to it. I do not know of one case where people benefited from the amendment made in 1940. I am also disappointed with the section 7 as suggested in this bill, because it also has strings attached to it. As soon as possible I should like either to have the strings removed, or to have the matter brought down to an individual basis.
I am also in agreement with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he suggests the removal of the 3,000 bushel limit. It is not many weeks since I made the same suggestion to the minister. I am firmly convinced that he, too, believes it should be removed. Apparently, however, as in other cases, some of his colleagues do not think as he does. I hope his colleagues may possibly give some greater attention to a fair deal, and have this limitation removed before the summer passes. It has been there for one year, and in my opinion that is one year too long. I should hope to see it removed before another session comes round.

I should like to add my
observations to those which have already been made in favour of the amendments. I believe they are all to the good. In the part of the province from which I come we did not come under this act until last year when, owing to frost in that section of the province, certain areas came within the scope of the act I was in hopes that the minister would bring in an amendment whereby in areas where grain was frozen and the price was very low, the number of bushels to the acre would be raised, to permit the farmers to come under the act. Instead of four, eight and twelve, I suggest that in respect of frozen grain, which has only about half the value of No. 1 wheat, this might be raised to eight, twelve and sixteen bushels. Has the minister given consideration to that point?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have, but the difficulty with legislation of this kind is, as hon. members are aware, that it is new legislation. I do not know of any other place where similar legislation is in effect. We had no experience to start with; we had to build up something entirely new. Our fear at the beginning was that every condition put into the legislation would increase the cost of administration, and we thought it would be quite easy to get the administrative costs so high that the legislation would be objectionable to government authorities generally. We have been trying to avoid that. To put in a condition to provide payment on other than a crop yield basis, on

Supply-Agriculture
the basis of wheat grades-if wheat were frozen and reduced to No. 4, a man would require to have more bushels-there would be so much in the way of added inspection costs that in due course that kind of thing would kill the legislation.
That was what was in our minds when we hesitated to do what was suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). They suggested that we use the quarter township right through. As you decrease the area taken as the unit, you increase the cost as well as the number of complaints. Most of our complaints are in connection with border-line cases. If you divide your township into four quarters, you have about 50 per cent more boundary line. The boundary lines are drawn down to such small proportions that you will have more farmers with land on both sides of the line. You will then run into trouble all the way round. It will also require extra inspection and extra checking and correspondence. All this would increase the cost of administration to a level where there would be criticism as to the cost.
One of the reasons why I feel that probably we made a mistake in inserting the 3,000 bushel provision last year is the fact that it has increased our inspection and administration costs. They will be almost double this year. If we go on doubling our costs of administration by inserting provisions that look reasonable on their faces, we shall eventually have the cost up so high and the criticism of the legislation will be so great that we shall probably lose it in the end. It is better to try to keep the costs of administration down to a reasonable point.
I went through the experience in 1914 and 1915 of establishing hail insurance legislation in western Canada. Hon. members who were in the west at that time will recall that there was far more criticism of that legislation than there is of this. But to-day one never hears any criticism. As people learn the regulations, as they learn what the legislation provides for. they fit their circumstances accordingly and cease to criticize. We are having the same experience with this legislation.

If we take that number of inspectors at $5 a day, it will be found that the average time they were employed was about seventy-four days, or a little over two months. Therefore when it is said that there are 281 inspectors, it does not mean they are working all the year. The others are all part-time employees tvho are put on during the rush season in the summer.

I should like to add my support to the submission of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle respecting a reduction in the present staff. I realize that there would be an increase in the administrative staff for the reason given by the minister, but I do not think that explanation is tenable so far as the inspectors are concerned. At a time like the present, when there should be conservation of our resources, the minister ought to make a special effort to reduce these expenses by placing more and more power in the control of the secretaries of the rural municipalities, who have the necessary data before them when the farmer comes to the municipality to secure his permit.
In connection with the inspectors I notice that one inspector, N. W. Berglund, of Melville, received a salary of $645, which means that he worked 109 days, and his expenses were $1,257.87, or an average of $11.50 a day. That seems to be an excessive amount of expenses.
I should like to deal for a moment with the regulations in effect under the provisions of the act. The act makes provision for every farmer contributing one per cent of the amount that he receives. I feel that the regulations should not be so drawn as to limit the purview of the application of the act. I am

going to refer to three regulations that were passed which limit the meaning of the word "farmer" as defined in the act. "Farmer" is defined in the act as "a person engaged in farming in the spring wheat area". But in the regulations the connotation of the term has been greatly modified. Section 8 of the regulations provides:
No person shall be considered to be a farmer under the act unless (1) he is owner or tenant of a farm from May 1 to November 1 in any year. . . ,
All of us know that there are written leases as well as verbal leases, but under the administration of this act farmers all over western Canada have been denied their bonus on account of the fact that their leases in writing were dated after May 1, in spite of the fact that they had a verbal lease prior to that date.
Next is subsection 2 of section 8 of the regulations which provides that no one can receive a bonus, even though he is a farmer, unless he lives on the farm and his primary occupation is farming, or he lives not more than twenty miles away from the farm and has no other occupation than farming. I know of instances-I have the particulars with me-of farmers who are engaged in other occupations who have received the bonus, and yet in other cases the regulations have been applied to prevent persons in a similar category from receiving the bonus.
Subsection 5 of section 8 provides that a person residing with a parent or a brother of the full age of twenty years and operating a farm as a separate unit, and the farm consisting of at least a quarter-section of land, shall be denied the bonus. There is no reason at all why a young man under twenty years of age who is farming his land should be denied the bonus, but he is to-day. The regulations as they are presently constituted abrogate the definition of "farmer" as it appears in the statute. Changes should be made in those regulations because they are most unfair and most discriminatory against bona fide farmers who under the act are entitled to the bonus, but under the regulations are not.
I would suggest that the recommendations made 'by the legislature of Saskatchewan should be brought into effect, and immediately, in order to do away with anomalies and inconsistencies in the administration of the act. The recommendations made by the legislature of Saskatchewan are as follows, and in those recommendations I concur:
(a)	That the bonus be paid on the individual farm unit or, as an alternative, that provision be made whereby a township can be divided into two or more parts for the purpose of paying the bonus awards.
