The objections to this regulation have to some extent been met as a result of the amendment introduced to-day. Then paragraph (b):
(b)	That subsection (b) of section 8 of the act be deleted.
(c)	That sections 3 and 4 in the act be made obligatory instead of permissive.
(d)	Repeal of the regulations under which dispossessed farmers are unable to receive bonus payment until they have signed a lease for the following year, such provision to include those who have enlisted in the armed forces and to be made retroactive to cover the 1940 crop.
I have already dealt with that phase of the matter, what I have called the discrimination against those who to-day are enlisting in the service of their country, which places them in a position where, unless they stay on their farms from the 1st of May to the 1st of November, they are denied participation in the fund.
(e)	Repeal of regulation prohibiting bonus payment to farmers who were in occupation of their farms previous to May 1, but who were unable to secure written lease until after May 1, this to apply to the 1940 crop.
(f)	Granting request of rural municipal council for reinspection to determine eligibility of bonus, this to be made retroactive for the 1940 crop.
(g)	That adequate representation be given to the producers on any board or commission appointed for the purpose of administration of this act.
I should like to have a statement from the minister as to whether the resolution passed by the legislature of Saskatchewan has been brought to his attention and what decision has been made by the government with respect to the implementation thereof.
I have referred to the regulations and their unfairness in interfering with the act and its application. That is not my opinion alone; it was the opinion of members of the legislature belonging to the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, who themselves introduced the resolution in the house and asked that these inconsistencies to which I have referred should be removed.
Mr. Danielson, the member for Arm River, said this:
The regulations were unreasonable, and they were . . . drafted by men who had not the least idea of what a western farm is like.
The newspaper report of his speech then is as follows:-
He stated further that the intent and purpose of the parliament of Canada when it passed the act were being thwarted by a bureaucratic and plutocratic civil service. He asserted that his remarks were not to be interpreted as a reflection upon the man in charge for he was doing his level best to carry on a difficult task, made difficult by unreasonable regulations drawn up by men who did not know whit they were doing.
Would the minister explain to the committee what the intention of the government -is in so for as the alteration of these regulations is concerned, so that the inconsistencies in administration may be done away with?
A great deal of good has been done under this legislation. I realize the difficulties of the minister, starting in a new field, but I think that now, after the experience of two years or more, the time is come when these regulations should be altered.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Just following the last remarks, I have here the regulations, and each one of these blue tabs represents an amendment. In the last two years we. have revised them nine different times, so that I can assure the hon. member that they are being revised from time to time as we have experience with them.
I read the recommendations of the Saskatchewan legislature shortly after they were passed, as they were sent to me. I do not happen to have them on my desk at the moment, and I do not know that I can remember them all. But, as was suggested, the first one refers to the question which was brought up by hon. members when the bill was in the house, namely, whether we should inspect all individual cases. I wish only to say with regard to that what I said when the bill was brought into the house in the first instance, and what our experience since has justified me in saying. I do not think this legislation would stay on the statute books for three years if we attempted to investigate all the individual cases. Those who recommend that have no idea at all of the principles of this act or how it was intended to operate. Their impression is that this measure was introduced for the purpose of giving assistance to wheat growers. The bill was not brought in for that purpose at all. Its object was to help those who were living in the drought areas, no matter what they were producing, so as .to assist them through the difficult drought period. In many of those districts farmers should be encouraged to decrease wheat acreage, or to get partly out of wheat growing and partly into something else. In other areas that would n'ot be the proper thing to encourage them to do; they are probably growing wheat to as good advantage as they could produce anything else. But if we were to place the act on an individual basis instead of the basis it is now on, we would have to inspect every individual case, and not only that, but we would have to take an inventory of everything the farmer produced on his farm during the year. To try to operate legislation of this kind on that basis, would simply make it altogether inoperative.

Supply-Agriculture

Wheat is used in connection with this legislation only as a measuring stick. We take a township of land, six miles square, and we say that if the yield of wheat in that area is under twelve bushels to the acre, they have had bad weather, and the bad weather is responsible for the low yield. We use wheat to determine the farming conditions in that area, and the man who grows no wheat at all in that area will have just as poor a crop of grass, or coarse grain, or something else, or will have just as difficult a time pasturing his cattle, as the man has who is growing the twelve bushels or less of wheat. We simply go over the area and say, because the average yield of wheat in that area is less than twelve bushels to the acre the farmer requires some assistance, and then we provide the assistance. The intention of this act to begin with was that we would pay assistance to every individual in that area.
My hon. friend over here, who does not farm in the west but in the east, struck the nail right on the head when he said that if you start to deal with individual cases on the basis of wheat acreage and wheat yield, you will put all of the good farmers out from under this act almost any year. The good farmers in those districts, particularly, let us say, in the central part of Saskatchewan, the northern part of Manitoba, and through the central and northern part of Alberta, are carrying on mixed farming, and they grow whatever wheat they do grow only in order to get a more or less sure cash crop, and they grow it on a comparatively small acreage, the best acreage they have-that is, best in preparation for that particular year's production. Such a man may grow twenty bushels to the acre of wheat, or he may grow even thirty bushels on a small acreage, and the remainder of his crop, which is a coarse grain crop put in on spring ploughing and his grass may all be poor because of poor moisture conditions during the latter part of June and July. He is more completely up against it, because he has live stock for which he has no feed, than even the wheat grower alongside him who grew nothing but wheat and got ten bushels to the acre in that particular year.
I say again that wheat is used only as a measuring stick, and to carry out this legislation under individual inspections would be absolutely impossible. The costs of carrying it out in that way would be so great that in three or four years' time this house would not maintain this legislation on the statute books.
The alternative proposal is the one we adopted this evening in the legislation. The legislature said, "Do one thing or the other."

We have undertaken to do the other, but we have not gone as far as the legislature suggested. They suggested that we reduce the units to the quarter township. When you go into a solid block of forty municipalities and the inspector drives over that and finds that it is all under twelve bushels, there is no necessity of going down farther than the complete area, although for convenience we divide the area into townships for administration. Sometimes there is an area round the rim, where there are better crop areas, and that is where all the inspection and checking have to be done. When we make that inspection and checking on the border-line, we take in or throw out quarter townships under the new legislation. We not only take in quarters out of the corner of the township, but we provide that a quarter township or more, so long as it is rectangular, shall come in as a separate township if it is under ten bushels to the acre. We have taken the alternative suggested by the legislature, and applied it as far as we can.
The second proposal is that paragraph (b) of section 8 of the act be deleted. That has to do with the 3,000 bushels, and we have decided not to delete it. The next is that sections 3 and 4 of the act be made obligatory instead of permissive. To all intents and purposes they are obligatory. The question that arises there is the same one that was under discussion between the leader of the opposition and myself early in the session in connection with another bill-that is, as to whether "may" means "shall" in certain cases. When this legislation was before the house at an earlier date, the same matter was under discussion. The then leader of the opposition Mr. Bennett, on the first occasion when it was discussed, took the position which I took earlier this session. When I took that position earlier in this session, the leader of the opposition checked it and sent me the book to indicate that Mr. Bennett had been right because, after all, I was quoting Mr. Bennett when I made the statement that in these cases "may" does mean "shall," and that these sections are obligatory. In other words, if all the conditions of the legislation are met in the area, then payment is made, and there is no way by which the minister can get out of making it.
Further, it is recommended that the regulations be repealed under which dispossessed farmers are unable to receive bonus payment. There is nothing in the regulations about it. A dispossessed farmer was refused payment, apparently, if he was put off the farm through foreclosure proceedings before he had received

Provincial Income and. Corporation Taxes
payment. Under the amendments brought in to-night he would lose payment only if he were put off the -farm before November 1, and hon. members will agree that it is not very often that farmers are removed from the land in the summer months when they are going on with their farming operations. The courts usually take care of that. The farmer will get by the first of November and receive payment if he is on the land from May 1 to November 1.
The next has reference to repeal of the regulations prohibiting bonus payment to farmers who were not in occupation of their farms prior to May 1. Of course, the difficulty which was discussed a few moments ago before this was read is involved in that suggestion. The provision now is, and has been since the act was first put on the statute books, that a man must be in control of the land by the 1st of May. The first year we allowed that to go even by word of mouth so long as they could establish it. The second year we stated that there must be a written contract. We had run into some difficulties because contracts were not signed until after the 1st of May, but in actual practice we have ruled that if a man can establish that he was living on the place on the 1st of May we make payment. It is true they were denied payment in the first instance, when they made their claims, if the contract read at a date later than May 1, but those who have come back and can prove that they were actually operating the land before the 1st of May, or on the 1st of May, have been allowed payment; and if any others have not been paid and are in the same position, they can prove their right to payment.

Suppose a farmer had a verbal lease whereby he was to have possession from the 1st of May, but his lease in writing was dated the 3rd of May and he did not go into possession until the 3rd of May? Would he be entitled to the bonus?

It will not take care of individuals who will not come in two or three days earlier in order to get claims which they later intend to make.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In tabling these estimates, I should perhaps say a word or two in explanation of the item relating to the proposal to the provinces to vacate the personal income and corporation tax fields for the duration of the war, ia ' order that there may be no misunderstanding aibout what is intended. It is estimated that if all provinces accept the proposal, the annual payments to them in accordance with the formula which I described in the budget speech will amount to approximately $80,000,000. It was never anticipated that the payments to be made by the dominion in the current fiscal year would be as much as this because of the lag or interval which will occur before existing provincial tax revenues stop coming in. Our original thought was that the dominion's payments to the provinces might begin towards the end of the present calendar year, but after discussing the matter with the representatives of a number of the provinces who have been in Ottawa, we reached the conclusion that a more accurate and uniform procedure would be necessary. Accordingly the intention is to date the arrangements with the provinces from the beginning of their present fiscal years. The dominion will deduct from the amounts which would otherwise be paid to them the taxes which the provinces and their municipalities collect after the beginning of the provinces' present fiscal years which apply to incomes of the year 1940 or prior years, or which are based upon the taxpayers' operations or status in the year 1940 or prior years. Without a provision of this sort the provinces would receive in their 1941-42 fiscal year payments from the dominion equivalent to their previous year's tax collections, and in addition they would collect a substantial amount of taxes which they themselves levied on incomes of 1940 and prior years.
Questions

The amount which will be withheld by the dominion under the proposed procedure will be paid over to the provinces in the year following the termination of the agreement and will provide funds for provincial requirements during the interval which will occur before new provincial tax revenues begin to come in.
I am planning to answer the questions put to me at the beginning of last week by the leader of the opposition (Mr, Hanson) when this item in the estimates is being considered in committee, but I thought this brief explanation was desirable at this stage in order to prevent any possible misunderstanding or misconception of what is proposed.
